Environmental Calculus 2 - Active Learning with Case Studies Gaj Sivandran 2026-10-31 Chapter 1 Why Calculus? In QSCI 291 you kept asking one question: how fast is this changing? This book asks the reverse. If you know the rate, can you work out the total? A stream gauge records discharge every 15 minutes during a storm. That’s a rate, in cubic meters per second. A flood manager wants a volume: how much water went past the gauge? A flux tower measures carbon exchange over a forest every half hour. Someone has to work out how much carbon that forest stored over the year. Going from a rate to a total is integration, and it’s most of this course. The last chapter turns the problem around again. Sometimes all you have is a rule for how something changes, like a pollutant that breaks down in proportion to how much is left. Differential equations let you work out where the system is headed from that rule alone. Welcome to Environmental Calculus 2. 1.1 Why This Book? Like the 291 book, this one puts environmental examples first. Physics shows up only when it makes an idea easier to feel. The problems come from things you could actually measure: streamflow, pollutant loads, carbon exchange, population change. 1.2 How This Book Works Each chapter mixes explanation, worked examples, concept checks and practice problems. Answers sit behind click-to-reveal blocks. Try the problem before you open them. That’s where the learning happens. The workbook chapters at the back give you more practice for each chapter, with answer keys. The equation sheet and test review material are there too. 1.3 Success in This Class First and foremost, know this: we believe in your ability to learn and grow. You bring unique strengths and perspectives, and your effort matters here. Mistakes are not a setback—they are the very heart of learning. When you get something wrong, you uncover where your thinking needs refinement, and that creates the space for real growth. Struggle is not a sign you don’t belong; it’s proof that your brain is stretching and building new connections. Just like in science, learning calculus is about iteration—trying, testing, revising, and improving. That process is what makes your understanding deeper and more durable. Assessments in this class are snapshots of your thinking at a particular moment in time. They are not final judgments about your intelligence, your worth, or your potential. You will have chances to revisit concepts, refine your understanding, and demonstrate what you’ve learned. Growth comes from re-engaging with the material, not from perfection on the first try. So give yourself permission to be imperfect. Keep engaging, reflecting, and asking questions. We’ll be here to support you every step of the way. 1.4 Looking Ahead By the end of this course, you will be able to: Apply calculus concepts to natural systems Analyze environmental data with confidence Interpret and communicate your results to others But even more important than any specific skill, you’ll leave this course with a stronger belief in your ability to learn mathematics. Calculus is not just a hurdle to clear—it’s a tool that expands how you see and understand the world. Our hope is that by connecting it to the environment you care about, you’ll discover both its usefulness and its beauty. Most importantly, you’ll leave with the confidence to keep growing—using mathematics as a tool to explore, protect, and better understand the natural world around you. 1.5 ⚠️ A Big Disclaimer ⚠️ I started writing this textbook to create a calculus resource that speaks directly to your interests as environmental scientists. My goal is to make calculus feel relevant, supportive, and connected to the systems you care about. That said, this is very much a work in progress. Chapter 2 Introduction to Calculus II A storm parks over a Pacific Northwest watershed. Rain falls — sometimes a drizzle, sometimes a downpour — and at the bottom of the basin, a stream gauge ticks upward. How much water passed the gauge over the storm? Out in the forest, a stand of Douglas-fir is pulling carbon out of the air. The rate of uptake shifts with the sun, the temperature, the time of day. How much carbon did the forest take up this summer? These are questions about totals, and in environmental science, totals matter. Calculus I gave you tools to describe how systems change moment by moment. Calculus II gives you tools to add those moments up. Welcome to Calculus II — the mathematics of accumulation. In Calculus I, you learned to describe how natural systems behave at a given moment: how fast a population is growing, how quickly temperature is changing, or how sharply a pollutant concentration shifts at a point in space. In this course, we shift the question: How much water flowed down a stream over the day? How much carbon did a forest take up this summer? How much nitrogen was exported from a watershed during a storm? How much biomass accumulated in a recovering ecosystem? These are questions about totals. Being able to quantify accumulation helps us understand environmental systems that are dynamic, interconnected, and continuously changing. This course is the second half of the Q SCI 291–292 sequence, which builds the mathematical foundation used across biology, ecology, conservation, marine science, and environmental science. Alongside the core mathematical ideas, the course emphasizes learning how to think quantitatively about real systems and developing the reasoning skills needed to communicate scientific results clearly. By the end of this course, you will be able to: Explain and interpret definite integrals using Riemann sums, limits, and graphical representations. Compute and apply integrals using substitution, integration by parts, and numerical methods to solve environmental and biological problems. Analyze and model natural systems using basic differential equations, including separable and first-order linear forms. Construct and justify clear mathematical reasoning — written, numerical, and graphical — so you can communicate solutions effectively and assess their validity. 2.1 What Calculus II Is Really About At its core, Calculus II is the study of accumulation. Many quantities in the natural world — heat, nutrients, biomass, pollutants, water, individuals — change continuously rather than in neat steps. When a quantity’s rate changes from moment to moment, how do we figure out the total amount gained or lost? Integrals give us the language and tools to answer that question. Calculus I asked: how fast is something changing? Calculus II asks: how much has accumulated? These two questions are inseparable — they are linked by one of the most beautiful results in mathematics, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. We’ll get there. System Calc I Question (rate) Calc II Question (total) Hydrology How fast is streamflow rising during a storm? How much water flowed past the gauge? Forests How fast is the canopy taking up CO₂ right now? How much carbon did the stand take up this summer? Populations What is the salmon population’s growth rate this week? How many fish passed the weir over the whole run? Toxicology How quickly is a contaminant entering a lake? How much contaminant has accumulated by year-end? Example: Accumulating Rainfall in a Simple Storm To anchor the idea of accumulation, imagine a 3-hour storm where the rainfall intensity stays constant within each hour. Suppose the observed intensities are: Hour 1: 4 mm/hour Hour 2: 7 mm/hour Hour 3: 5 mm/hour If the rainfall rate is constant within each hour, the total rainfall is simply: \[ \text{Total rainfall} = 4 + 7 + 5 = 16 \text{ mm}. \] Each bar represents the amount of rain added during one hour. The total rainfall is the sum of these three rectangular blocks. This situation is straightforward because each hour contributes a clean, fixed amount of rainfall. When Rainfall Intensity Is Not Constant Real storms rarely behave this neatly. Rainfall intensity rises, falls, and fluctuates as storm cells pass overhead. Instead of three flat bars, the intensity becomes a wiggly, continuously changing curve. This leads us to the central question of the course: How much total rain falls during a storm like this? There are no neat hourly blocks anymore. The rainfall rate rises, dips, oscillates, and never sits still long enough for a simple calculation. To find the total, we need a method that can add up many small and continuously changing contributions. A key insight is that large totals often come from accumulating many small pieces. This is intuitive when you think about rainfall or streamflow, and it’s the conceptual foundation of Riemann sums and definite integrals. We won’t dive into the technical details yet, but this perspective will guide us throughout the course — it’s the bridge that connects data, graphs, equations, and models. Another major theme is reversing derivatives. If a derivative tells us how a quantity is changing, an antiderivative recovers the original quantity. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus ties these ideas together and is the foundation of the integration techniques you’ll learn. Finally, many environmental and biological systems follow rules of change. Populations grow or decline, chemicals decay, temperatures level out, and nutrients move through ecosystems. These processes can be described using differential equations — mathematical stories of how systems evolve. In this course we’ll work with simple and powerful forms (especially separable and first-order linear equations) that let us model natural processes clearly and effectively. Concept Check: Rate vs. Total For each question below, decide whether the quantity being asked about is a rate of change (derivative-flavored) or an accumulation (integral-flavored). 1. A weather station reports that rain is currently falling at 8 mm/hour. Is this a rate or an accumulation? Click to reveal answer This is a rate — it tells you how fast water is arriving right now, in mm per hour. A derivative-flavored quantity. 2. A storm has produced 42 mm of rain over the past 6 hours. Is this a rate or an accumulation? Click to reveal answer This is an accumulation — it tells you the total rain that has piled up over a period of time. An integral-flavored quantity. 3. A salmon counting station records that fish are passing at 120 fish per day during the peak of the run. Is this a rate or an accumulation? Click to reveal answer This is a rate — fish per day is a rate, no matter how many days the run lasts. 4. Over the whole season, 38,000 salmon passed the counting station. Is this a rate or an accumulation? Click to reveal answer This is an accumulation — the seasonal total is what you get by adding up the daily counts (an integral of the rate over the season). 2.2 What You Bring From Calculus I You already have most of the ingredients you need. Calculus I gave you: A feel for how to read and interpret graphs A working understanding of derivatives as rates of change The ability to recognize when a quantity is increasing, decreasing, leveling off, or turning around Practice working with functions and equations flexibly You’ll also find that clean algebra makes a big difference. Rearranging equations, factoring, simplifying expressions, and solving for unknowns are routine steps in almost every meaningful Calc 2 calculation. Strengthening these skills now will make the deeper ideas of this course much more accessible. 2.3 Big Themes of the Course 2.3.1 Accumulation Many environmental processes unfold gradually, not in discrete chunks. Rainfall builds up drop by drop. A stream transports nutrients continuously. Forests take up carbon throughout the day as light changes. In all of these situations, the total amount that accumulates is the result of many small contributions happening moment by moment. Integrals give us a framework for quantifying these cumulative effects. When a rate varies across time, space, or depth, an integral lets us add up tiny pieces into a meaningful whole. This perspective is essential in environmental science, where totals often tell us more about system behavior than any single measurement. A few examples to keep in mind as you read the rest of the course: Total nitrogen export from a watershed. Streamflow and nutrient concentration both change during storms. The total mass exported is not the peak concentration times the storm duration — it’s the accumulation of many changing contributions as water moves through the system. Total phytoplankton production over a day. Photosynthesis depends on light, which changes continuously with cloud cover and solar angle. The daily production is the sum of many small increments of carbon fixed throughout the day. Energy exchanged in an ocean mixed layer. Heat flux varies with wind, sunlight, and water temperature. Understanding how much energy enters or leaves the ocean requires accumulating many small changes over time. Accumulation is one of the central ideas of this course. Integrals appear throughout Calc 2 not just as procedures to learn, but as conceptual tools for interpreting how environmental systems grow, shrink, cycle, and respond to change. Concept Check: Recognizing Accumulation For each of the following, ask yourself: am I being told a rate, or a total? 1. A research vessel logs that sea-surface heat flux into the mixed layer was 180 W/m² yesterday at noon. To find the total energy that entered a 1 m² patch of ocean over a 24-hour period, what kind of operation do you need to do? Click to reveal answer You need to accumulate (integrate) the heat flux over the 24-hour period. The flux is a rate (W/m² = J/s/m²), and totaling it over time gives you the total energy delivered (J/m²). You couldn’t just multiply 180 × 24 × 3600 unless the flux were constant — which it isn’t, because sunlight varies through the day. 2. A pollutant enters a lake from a single inflow stream. You have continuous measurements of the inflow rate (m³/s) and the pollutant concentration (mg/L) every minute. To compute the total mass of pollutant delivered to the lake over a week, what are you doing conceptually? Click to reveal answer You’re accumulating many small contributions. At each minute, the rate of mass entering is roughly (concentration) × (flow rate). Multiplying that by the small time interval gives a small mass increment, and summing all of those increments over the week gives the total mass — exactly the structure of an integral. 2.3.2 Reversing Derivatives: Antiderivatives and the Fundamental Idea A derivative describes how something changes at each moment. An integral describes how much has changed in total. These two ideas are connected through antiderivatives, which let us reverse the process of differentiation. This relationship is one of the central insights of Calculus II and the foundation of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. In environmental terms: a rate of change is often easier to measure or model than the total amount. Antiderivatives give us a way to move from the rate back to the accumulated quantity. 2.3.2.1 Why This Connection Matters In environmental science, we often measure or model rates: the rate at which pollutants decay the rate of heat transfer into a lake the rate at which a population grows the rate of oxygen consumption in soil But what we usually care about are the totals: total pollutant remaining total heat gained total change in population total oxygen used Antiderivatives are the bridge between how something changes and how much it has changed overall. This connection is the conceptual heart of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and it’s why derivatives and integrals — though they look different — are deeply linked. Concept Check: From Rate to Total A field crew measures soil respiration (the rate at which microbes release CO₂) every 15 minutes for a full day. They get a function \(R(t)\), in grams of carbon per square meter per hour, that varies through the day with temperature and moisture. 1. To get the total carbon released over the 24-hour period, what do they do with \(R(t)\) conceptually? Click to reveal answer They integrate \(R(t)\) over the 24-hour interval. Each small time slice \(\Delta t\) contributes roughly \(R(t)\,\Delta t\) grams of carbon per square meter, and summing all those contributions (in the limit as the slices get small) gives the total accumulated release. 2. Suppose instead they have a function \(C(t)\) that tells them the total carbon released up to time \(t\). What does \(C'(t)\) represent? Click to reveal answer \(C'(t)\) is the instantaneous rate of carbon release at time \(t\) — which is exactly \(R(t)\). This is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in action: differentiating the accumulation gives back the rate. 2.3.3 Change Over Time: A First Look at Differential Equations Many natural systems evolve according to rules that describe how things change rather than simply giving their values at any moment. A population grows because new individuals are added. A pollutant decays because chemical reactions reduce its concentration. A lake warms or cools because heat is exchanged with the environment. In each case, the rate at which a quantity changes is often easier to understand, measure, or model than the total amount itself. Differential equations provide a mathematical framework for capturing these rules of change. Instead of expressing a relationship between quantities alone, a differential equation expresses a relationship between a quantity and its rate of change. This lets us describe dynamic systems that respond to their own current state: Population growth may speed up when populations are small, slow down when resources become limited, or collapse under stress. Chemical concentrations may decline at a rate that depends on how much of the substance is present. Heat transfer may proceed quickly when temperature differences are large, and more slowly as equilibrium is approached. Nutrients may cycle through ecosystems at rates that depend on biological activity, temperature, or moisture. These processes share a common feature: the present state of the system determines how it will change next. Differential equations make that dependency explicit. At this stage, the goal isn’t to solve differential equations — it’s to recognize what they represent. A differential equation is essentially a rulebook for how a system responds over time. It tells us: whether the system is increasing or decreasing, whether the change is fast or slow, how the rate of change varies with context, and what long-term behaviors might emerge. Later in the course you’ll learn techniques for solving differential equations and writing their solutions in closed form. For now, it’s enough to recognize that they’re a way of translating scientific understanding into mathematical language — moving from descriptions like “the population grows faster when resources are abundant” to precise statements that can be analyzed, simulated, and interpreted. Concept Check: Recognizing a Differential Equation Which of the following statements describe a differential equation — meaning they express a rate of change in terms of the quantity itself (or some other rate)? 1. “The size of a fish population at year 10 is 4,200 individuals.” Click to reveal answer Not a differential equation — this is just a snapshot of the population at a single point in time. There’s no rate of change in the statement. 2. “A pollutant decays at a rate proportional to the amount currently present.” Click to reveal answer Yes — this is a differential equation in words. Mathematically: \(\dfrac{dC}{dt} = -kC\), where \(C\) is the concentration. The rate \(\dfrac{dC}{dt}\) depends on the current amount \(C\). 3. “The temperature of a small pond changes at a rate proportional to the difference between the pond temperature and the surrounding air temperature.” Click to reveal answer Yes — also a differential equation. This is Newton’s Law of Cooling: \(\dfrac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_{\text{air}})\). The rate of change depends on the current state. 2.3.4 Skills That Make Calculus II Easier Solving equations and rearranging expressions Sketching functions and recognizing trends Keeping track of context — what’s changing, and what the units represent Strengthening these skills frees up your attention for the new ideas in this course. 2.4 Building an Intuition for Accumulation Before we compute any integrals, it helps to develop a clear intuition for how totals arise from variable rates. Many environmental quantities don’t behave uniformly. Streamflow responds to storms. Photosynthesis rises and falls with sunlight. Pollutant concentration shifts with depth and time. Populations grow quickly under some conditions and slowly under others. A useful way to think about accumulation is to imagine that each small moment in time — or each small slice of space — contributes a tiny amount to the total. When we add all those contributions together, we get a meaningful quantity: total rainfall, total biomass added, total pollutant exported. This perspective is why the integral has the structure it does, and why graphical reasoning plays such an important role in this course. Each colored slice has a tiny width and a height equal to the rate at that location. Multiplying width by height gives the small contribution from that slice. Adding up all the slices — and, eventually, taking the limit as the slices become very thin — is how we’ll build up the idea of an integral. Graphical reasoning is especially powerful here. Without doing any calculations, a graph can show whether a system is gaining or losing, whether accumulation is happening quickly or slowly, and whether changes are steady or fluctuating. Throughout the course, we’ll use graphs not only to visualize functions but to interpret integrals, predict behavior, and communicate reasoning. Concept Check: Slicing Up an Accumulation Suppose you’re trying to estimate the total volume of water that flowed past a stream gauge during a 6-hour storm. You have flow measurements (in m³/s) recorded every 15 minutes. 1. To estimate the total volume, what would you do with each measurement? Click to reveal answer For each 15-minute interval, multiply the flow rate (m³/s) by the length of the interval (15 minutes = 900 seconds). That gives an approximate volume in m³ for that interval. Then sum all the small volumes across the 6-hour storm. This is the Riemann sum idea: each slice contributes width × height, and summing gives an estimate of the total. 2. If you instead had measurements every 1 minute, would your total be more or less accurate? Click to reveal answer More accurate. Smaller time slices capture the variation in flow rate more faithfully — there’s less chance of missing a rapid surge or assuming the rate stayed constant when it didn’t. The limit of this process, as the slice width shrinks toward zero, is the definite integral. 2.5 Units and Interpretation Units play a quietly important role in this course. Because integrals correspond to real physical quantities, understanding them means paying careful attention to what’s being measured and how the units combine. A few patterns worth recognizing now: Integrating a rate measured in “individuals per year” over time gives “individuals.” Integrating “mg/L × m³/s” gives a pollutant load measured in “mg/s,” and integrating that over a time interval gives total mass in milligrams. Integrating “W/m²” over time yields energy density in joules per square meter. Recognizing this structure is what makes results meaningful and consistent with the scientific context. Thinking in small pieces, drawing graphs, and tracking units are the three habits that make the formal definition of the integral feel natural once we introduce it. Concept Check: Tracking Units of an Accumulation 1. A wind turbine’s instantaneous power output is measured in kilowatts (kW = kJ/s). If you integrate this power over a 24-hour period, what are the units of your result? Click to reveal answer You get energy. If you integrate kW over hours, the natural unit is kilowatt-hours (kWh). If you integrate kW (= kJ/s) over seconds, the result is kilojoules (kJ). Either way, the “per time” in the rate cancels with the time you integrate over, leaving you with a total energy. 2. A scientist integrates a function with units of “kg of carbon per hectare per year” over a region measured in hectares, and then over a time interval measured in years. What are the units of the final result? Click to reveal answer Kilograms of carbon (kg C). Integrating over hectares cancels the “per hectare” and leaves kg/year. Integrating that over years cancels the “per year” and leaves just kg. 2.6 Looking Ahead As the course unfolds, you’ll learn how to compute integrals efficiently, how to solve differential equations that describe natural systems, and how to analyze environmental processes using a combination of mathematics, graphs, and scientific reasoning. More importantly, you’ll develop the ability to connect mathematical results back to the real-world systems they describe — a skill that’s essential in every corner of environmental science. Calculus II isn’t just about mastering techniques. It’s about learning to see the world through a quantitative lens: to understand how change accumulates, how systems evolve, and how mathematics can illuminate the patterns and processes that shape the natural environment. Welcome to the journey.

Chapter 3 What Is an Integral? A storm has been hammering the foothills for six hours, and a stream gauge at the bottom of the watershed has been logging flow rates the whole time. Each reading tells you how fast water is moving past — but the question your downstream community actually cares about is how much water has gone by. To answer that, you need to take all those changing flow rates and add them up across the storm. That is an integral. In Calculus I you learned to ask how fast is something changing right now? In Calculus II we shift the question to how much has accumulated? These two questions are inseparable — they are linked by one of the most beautiful results in mathematics, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. We’ll get there. For now, the goal of this chapter is to build up the integral one small piece at a time, starting from concrete environmental scenarios and ending with the formal Riemann-sum machinery. 3.1 Chapter Objectives By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: Explain how integrals model total accumulation in environmental systems and describe real-world examples such as streamflow, photosynthesis, and pollutant load. Interpret the area under a rate curve as a measure of total change, including situations with gains, losses, and mixed-sign behavior. Construct and evaluate Riemann sums (left, right, and midpoint) to approximate accumulation from graphical or numerical data. Use antiderivatives and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (informal version) to compute definite integrals representing environmental totals. Analyze and interpret accumulation functions to understand how totals build up over time in ecological and physical processes. 3.2 Accumulation in Environmental Systems Many natural processes are described not by totals but by rates — how fast something is happening. Integrals allow us to turn a rate into a total amount. Common environmental examples include: Streamflow → total river discharge over a day Photosynthesis rate → total daily carbon uptake Pollutant concentration × flow → total pollutant load entering a lake Evapotranspiration → total water loss during a heatwave Recruitment rate → total new individuals added to a population Key idea: If you know the rate at which something changes, the integral gives you the total change over a chosen interval. Walking on a Treadmill Imagine you’re walking on a treadmill at a steady speed of 5 miles per hour. This speed is a rate — it tells you how fast distance is being added as you move. If you walk at 5 mph for 1 hour, your total distance is: \[ \text{distance} = \text{rate} \times \text{time} = 5 \times 1 = 5 \text{ miles}. \] But even if the speed changes during the workout — maybe 4 mph during the warm-up, 5 mph in the middle, and 6 mph at the end — you can still find the total distance by adding up all the little pieces: each minute at 4 mph contributes a small amount of distance, each minute at 5 mph contributes a bit more, each minute at 6 mph contributes even more. When we add all these tiny contributions together, we get the total distance walked. This is exactly what an integral does: it adds up the accumulation of a changing rate over time. Concept Check: What an Integral Represents In your own words, what does an integral represent in environmental science? Click to reveal answer An integral represents the total accumulation of a quantity over time or space when the rate of change is known. It adds up many small contributions to determine a total amount — total volume of water, total carbon fixed, total mass exported, and so on. Concept Check: Why Rates Are Easier Than Totals Why are rates often easier to measure directly than total accumulated quantities? Click to reveal answer Rates can be measured instantaneously or over short intervals — a stream gauge logs discharge every few minutes, a flux tower logs CO₂ uptake at high frequency. Totals require tracking accumulation continuously over time or space, which is exactly what an integral does for us mathematically. 3.3 From Rate Curves to Areas Under Curves When we graph a rate \(f(t)\), the height of the curve represents how fast the system is changing at each moment. The total accumulation from time \(a\) to \(b\) is the area under the rate curve: Height (rate) × width (time) = accumulated amount Units multiply: \(\text{m}^3/\text{s} \times \text{s} = \text{m}^3\) \(\mu\text{mol}/(\text{m}^2\cdot\text{s}) \times \text{s} = \mu\text{mol}/\text{m}^2\) Environmental examples: Total river discharge from a storm hydrograph Total CO₂ absorbed during a sunny day Total nitrogen mineralized over a growing season Filling a Water Bottle Suppose you are filling a water bottle from a faucet, and the flow rate changes over time. At first, you turn the faucet on gently, and water flows at 50 mL/s. A few seconds later, you open it more, and the flow increases to 90 mL/s. Near the end, you partially close it, slowing the flow to 30 mL/s. If you graph this changing flow rate over time, the height of the curve at any moment shows how quickly water is entering the bottle. To find out how much water ends up in the bottle, you do not multiply a single rate by a single time. Instead, you add up: a small amount of water from the low initial rate, a larger amount from the high middle rate, a small amount again when the flow slows down. On the graph, these “small amounts” correspond to thin rectangles under the curve. Adding them all together gives the area under the rate curve, which equals the total volume of water in the bottle. This is exactly what an integral measures: the total accumulation obtained by adding up tiny contributions from a changing rate. Concept Check: Area Under a Rate Curve What does the area under a rate curve represent? Click to reveal answer The area under a rate curve represents the total accumulated change of the quantity over the interval shown. If the rate is m³/s and the horizontal axis is seconds, the area has units of m³ — a volume. Concept Check: Why the Units Work Out Why do the units of an integral make sense physically? Click to reveal answer Because the integral multiplies a rate by a width (time or distance), the units simplify to a total quantity. For example, m³/hr × hr = m³, mg C/m²/day × day = mg C/m², and so on. The “per time” or “per distance” in the rate cancels with the variable you’re integrating over. Concept Check: Why a Single Rate Times Time Falls Short Why is multiplying a single rate by total time often a poor approximation in environmental systems? Click to reveal answer Because rates in environmental systems usually change over time — streamflow rises and falls during a storm, photosynthesis depends on light, soil respiration depends on temperature. A single rate snapshot does not accurately represent the entire interval, so multiplying it by the full duration ignores all of that variation. 3.4 Riemann Sums: Adding Up Small Pieces In most real situations, rates are not constant. Streamflow rises and falls during a storm, photosynthesis changes throughout the day, and pollutant inputs vary with human activity. Because of this, we cannot usually find total accumulation by multiplying a single rate by a single time. Instead, we approximate accumulation by breaking the interval into many small pieces and adding up their individual contributions. The basic idea works as follows: Divide the interval into smaller subintervals of equal width. Approximate the rate as constant over each subinterval. Compute each slice’s contribution using \[ \text{(height)} \times \text{(width)}. \] Add all slices together to estimate the total accumulation. Each slice represents a small amount of accumulated quantity over a short period of time. When we add them all together, we get an approximation of the total. 3.4.1 Choosing a Riemann Sum Method The difference between left, right, and midpoint Riemann sums is not just mathematical—it reflects assumptions about how a system behaves within each subinterval. Choosing a method means deciding when you think the rate best represents the entire slice. Left Riemann sum: Uses the rate at the left endpoint of each subinterval. This method assumes the rate remains approximately constant at its initial value over the slice. It is most appropriate when: the rate is slowly changing, or you want a conservative or early estimate, or measurements are taken at the start of each interval. Common outcomes: Tends to underestimate accumulation when the rate is increasing. Tends to overestimate accumulation when the rate is decreasing. Environmental examples: Estimating pollutant inflow immediately after a spill Using early-morning evapotranspiration rates to estimate daily loss Right Riemann sum: Uses the rate at the right endpoint of each subinterval. This method assumes the rate has already changed to its later value by the start of the slice. It is most appropriate when: the process intensifies over time, or data are collected at the end of each interval, or you want a precautionary upper estimate. Common outcomes: Tends to overestimate accumulation when the rate is increasing. Tends to underestimate accumulation when the rate is decreasing. Environmental examples: Estimating peak streamflow during the rising limb of a storm Modeling afternoon photosynthesis after sunlight has increased Midpoint Riemann sum: Uses the rate at the midpoint of each subinterval. This method assumes the midpoint rate best represents the average behavior of the system over the slice. It is often preferred when: the rate changes smoothly, and no strong justification exists for early or late sampling, or higher accuracy is desired without increasing the number of slices. Common outcomes: Usually provides a better balance between over- and underestimation. Often converges to the true value faster than left or right sums. Environmental examples: Estimating daily carbon uptake from smoothly varying light levels Approximating total nitrogen mineralization over a growing season 3.4.2 A Practical Guideline When in doubt: Use left or right sums to reflect specific assumptions about timing or uncertainty. Use the midpoint sum as a reliable default for smooth, continuous processes. Increase the number of subintervals when accuracy matters more than simplicity. These choices highlight that Riemann sums are not just numerical tools—they are models of how we believe the system behaves between measurements. Click to reveal answer Each rectangle represents a small contribution to the total accumulation over a short subinterval. Its width is a small slice of time (or distance), and its height is the rate during that slice — multiplied together, they approximate the amount accumulated during that little window. Concept Check: Why More Rectangles Helps Why do Riemann sums become more accurate as the number of rectangles increases? Click to reveal answer Because smaller subintervals reduce how much the rate can change within each rectangle. The constant-rate assumption inside each subinterval becomes more reasonable when the subintervals are short, so the approximation closes in on the true accumulation. Concept Check: The Assumption Inside Each Rectangle What assumption is made when using rectangular approximations? Click to reveal answer That the rate remains approximately constant within each subinterval. Whether you sample at the left endpoint, right endpoint, or midpoint, you’re using that single value as a stand-in for the rate across the whole slice. 3.5 Approximation and Error in Riemann Sums It is important to be clear about what Riemann sums are — and what they are not. A Riemann sum is an approximation, not an exact calculation. By replacing a continuously changing rate with a set of constant rectangles, we introduce error. Each rectangle is only an estimate of what the curve is doing over that interval. The error comes from a simple source: The rectangles do not perfectly match the shape of the curve. Some rectangles extend above the curve, while others fall below it. The difference between the total area of the rectangles and the true area under the curve is called the approximation error. 3.5.1 Why Error Occurs Error arises because we make two simplifying assumptions: The rate is treated as constant within each subinterval. The true rate may be increasing, decreasing, or curved within that interval. If the curve bends significantly, wide rectangles can miss important changes. This is why Riemann sums improve when: subintervals are narrower, and more rectangles are used. In the limit, as the width of each subinterval approaches zero, the Riemann sum approaches the definite integral, which represents the exact accumulation. 3.5.2 Overestimates and Underestimates Whether a Riemann sum overestimates or underestimates the true accumulation depends on both: the shape of the rate curve, and the method used to choose rectangle heights. 3.5.2.1 Increasing Rate Functions When the rate is increasing over an interval: Left Riemann sums tend to underestimate the total accumulation, because each rectangle uses a rate that is smaller than most of the values in the interval. Right Riemann sums tend to overestimate the total accumulation, because they use a larger rate that occurs later in the interval. Midpoint Riemann sums usually balance these effects and provide a closer estimate. 3.5.2.2 Decreasing Rate Functions When the rate is decreasing over an interval: Left Riemann sums tend to overestimate the total accumulation. Right Riemann sums tend to underestimate the total accumulation. Midpoint Riemann sums again often provide a more accurate estimate. Concept Check: Why Left Sums Underestimate Increasing Rates Why does a left Riemann sum tend to underestimate accumulation for an increasing function? Click to reveal answer Because it uses the rate at the beginning of each interval, which is smaller than most values of the rate over that interval. Each rectangle’s height is set too low, and the cumulative underestimate adds up across all subintervals. Concept Check: Why Right Sums Overestimate Increasing Rates Why does a right Riemann sum tend to overestimate accumulation for an increasing function? Click to reveal answer Because it uses the rate at the end of each interval, which is larger than most values of the rate over that interval. Each rectangle’s height is set too high, and the cumulative overestimate adds up across all subintervals. Concept Check: Why the Midpoint Tends to Win Why is the midpoint Riemann sum often more accurate than left or right sums? Click to reveal answer Because the midpoint value often better represents the average behavior of the rate over the subinterval. For a smooth function, the portion of the rectangle that overshoots the curve on one side tends to cancel out the portion that undershoots on the other. 3.5.3 Interpreting Error in Environmental Contexts In environmental science, these distinctions are not just mathematical—they have real consequences. An underestimate of pollutant load may delay mitigation or regulatory action, while an overestimate of available water can lead to management plans that are unsustainable in practice. Each choice reflects assumptions about timing, uncertainty, and acceptable risk. For this reason, understanding how and why Riemann sums approximate accumulation is just as important as knowing how to compute them. In many real-world settings, the objective is not to find a perfectly exact value, but to make a safe, informed, and defensible decision. Under these conditions, deliberately choosing an overestimate or an underestimate is not an error—it is a purposeful modeling choice. Riemann sums make this choice explicit by allowing us to decide how the rate is sampled within each interval, and therefore how conservative our estimate will be. 3.5.3.1 Conservativeness and Decision-Making A conservative estimate is one that reduces risk by erring on the side of caution. Whether this means overestimating or underestimating depends entirely on the context and the consequences of being wrong. The key question is: What is worse: overestimating or underestimating the true accumulation? 3.5.3.2 When an Underestimate Is Conservative An underestimate is conservative when overstating the quantity could lead to harm, wasted resources, or unrealistic expectations. Examples include: Water supply planning: Underestimating total available water avoids promising more water than can reliably be delivered. Carbon sequestration estimates: Underestimating carbon uptake prevents overstating climate mitigation benefits. Wildlife population growth: Underestimating recruitment avoids overconfidence in population recovery. In these cases, a left or right Riemann sum may be chosen specifically because it produces a lower bound on the true value. 3.5.3.3 When an Overestimate Is Conservative An overestimate is conservative when underestimating the quantity could lead to insufficient protection or preparedness. Examples include: Pollutant load calculations: Overestimating pollutant input ensures regulations are strict enough to protect ecosystems. Flood risk assessment: Overestimating peak discharge supports safer infrastructure design. Resource demand forecasting: Overestimating energy or water demand helps prevent shortages. Here, an overestimate functions as a precautionary upper bound, prioritizing safety over efficiency. 3.5.3.4 Choosing a Method Intentionally Riemann sums make the assumptions behind these choices transparent: Left Riemann sums may provide conservative lower or upper bounds depending on whether the rate is increasing or decreasing. Right Riemann sums provide the opposite bound. Midpoint Riemann sums aim for accuracy rather than conservativeness. Choosing a method is therefore not just a mathematical step — it is a modeling decision that reflects values, priorities, and acceptable risk. 3.5.3.5 Key Takeaway Overestimates and underestimates are not mistakes. They are tools. By understanding how and why approximation error occurs, we can choose methods that align with the ethical, environmental, and practical consequences of our decisions.
