The FTC is a fast way to compute something already defined through limits of sums. 4.7 The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part II) Up to this point, we have built integrals from the ground up: as sums of small pieces, as limits of better and better approximations, and as accumulation driven by a changing rate. All of that work answered an important conceptual question: What does an integral mean? Part II of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus answers a different question: How do we compute an integral efficiently and exactly? Rather than adding infinitely many tiny rectangles by hand, the theorem shows that accumulated change can be found by working with an antiderivative. At its core, the theorem states: \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a), \] where \(F'(x) = f(x)\). This formula is powerful — but it only makes sense because of everything that came before. 4.7.1 Step 1: Accumulation Is a Function Fix a starting point \(a\), and define a function: \[ A(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt. \] This function represents: the total accumulated change from \(a\) to \(x\), built from the rate \(f(t)\), using the ideas of Riemann sums and limits. From Part I of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we know: \[ A'(x) = f(x). \] That is, the derivative of the accumulation function equals the rate. So \(A(x)\) is an antiderivative of \(f(x)\). 4.7.2 Step 2: Antiderivatives Are Not Unique There is only one derivative for a function. However, there are an infintie number of antiderivates. Lets see if we can understand this graphically. The figures below show two paired examples. In each pair: The left panel shows a rate function. The right panel shows several possible antiderivatives of that rate. These pairs illustrate two equally important ideas: The right-hand curves are antiderivatives of the left-hand curve. The left-hand curve is the derivative of every curve on the right. Both perspectives matter. Example 1: A Linear Streamflow Rate — \(f(t) = t\) Consider a small drainage channel where the flow rate rises linearly with time during the rising limb of a storm: \[ f(t) = t \quad \text{(mL/s)}, \] with \(t\) measured in seconds. The accumulated volume of water that has passed through the channel from time zero up to time \(t\) is an antiderivative of this rate: \[ F(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}t^2 + C, \] where the constant \(C\) represents the volume that had already passed before we started timing — different storms (or different starting moments) give different \(C\) values, but the shape of the accumulation curve is the same. In this example: The left panel shows the flow rate \(f(t) = t\). The right panel shows several cumulative-volume curves of the form \[ F(t) = \tfrac12 t^2 + C. \] All three curves on the right have different vertical positions but the same shape. Why? The slope of each curve at any time \(t\) is exactly \(t\) mL/s. That slope matches the height of the rate curve on the left. So: If you start with the rate \(f(t) = t\) and accumulate, you get a parabola. If you start with any of the parabolas on the right and differentiate, you recover the line \(f(t) = t\). The constant \(C\) only changes where the cumulative volume started — it doesn’t change how fast volume is accumulating at any moment. Example 2: A Net Carbon Flux That Switches Sign — \(f(t) = t^2 - 2\) Now consider a more realistic environmental rate. A flux tower in a young forest stand records net ecosystem carbon exchange during the first few hours after dawn, modeled as \[ f(t) = t^2 - 2 \quad \text{(mg C / m}^2\text{/hr)}, \] where \(t\) is hours after dawn. For \(t < \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\) hours the rate is negative — respiration is outpacing photosynthesis and the stand is losing carbon. After \(t = \sqrt{2}\), photosynthesis dominates and the stand starts gaining carbon. The cumulative carbon balance is an antiderivative of this rate: \[ F(t) = \tfrac{1}{3}t^3 - 2t + C, \] where \(C\) is the cumulative balance at the moment we started recording. In this example: The left panel shows the net flux rate \(f(t) = t^2 - 2\). It is negative early (the stand is a carbon source) and positive later (the stand is a sink). The right panel shows three cumulative carbon balance curves of the form \[ F(t) = \tfrac{1}{3} t^3 - 2t + C. \] Each cumulative-balance curve dips in the early hours (carbon being lost) and recovers after \(t = \sqrt{2}\) (carbon being gained back). Different starting balances \(C\) shift the curve up or down — but all three have: the same slope at every \(t\), equal to \(f(t)\), and the same turning point at \(t = \sqrt{2}\), where the flux flips sign. The differences between these curves come from different initial balances. What they share — the shape, the slopes, the location of the minimum — is exactly what the rate function dictates. The Two-Way Relationship These examples highlight a key idea of calculus: Differentiation moves from accumulation to rate. Integration moves from rate to accumulation. The left panel answers the question: How fast is the quantity changing right now? The right panel answers the question: How much has the quantity changed overall? They are two views of the same process. 4.7.3 Step 3: Why the Constant Does Not Matter for Definite Integrals The definite integral \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \] asks: How much has accumulated between \(x = a\) and \(x = b\)? Using the accumulation function: \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = A(b) - A(a). \] But since \(F(x) = A(x) + C\), \[ F(b) - F(a) = [A(b) + C] - [A(a) + C]. \] The constant cancels: \[ F(b) - F(a) = A(b) - A(a). \] So any antiderivative produces the same net change, even if it is shifted up or down. 4.7.4 Step 4: What the Formula Is Really Saying When we write: \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a), \] we are not using a shortcut or a trick. We are doing the following: building accumulation conceptually (Part I), recognizing that accumulation is an antiderivative, and measuring how much that accumulation changes over an interval. The formula works because integration and differentiation are inverse processes, not because we memorized a rule. 4.7.5 Key Takeaway The definite integral measures net accumulated change. Antiderivatives allow us to compute that change exactly, because subtracting values automatically removes any constant offset. This is why the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is not just a computational tool — it is a precise statement about how rates, accumulation, and change are connected. 4.7.6 What the Formula Means The expression \[ F(b) - F(a) \] should be read as: \(F(a)\): the accumulated amount up to the starting point \(F(b)\): the accumulated amount up to the ending point The difference: how much was added (or removed) between \(a\) and \(b\) In other words: A definite integral measures change, not just area. 4.7.7 Key Skills You Will Use 1. Identifying Antiderivatives To apply the theorem, you must recognize or compute a function \(F(x)\) such that: \[ F'(x) = f(x). \] This draws directly on your derivative knowledge from Calculus I. Examples: If \(f(x) = x^2\), then \(F(x) = \tfrac{x^3}{3}\). If \(f(x) = \sin x\), then \(F(x) = -\cos x\). If \(f(x) = e^x\), then \(F(x) = e^x\). 2. Evaluating at the Bounds Once an antiderivative is found: Evaluate it at the upper bound \(b\). Evaluate it at the lower bound \(a\). Subtract: \[ F(b) - F(a). \] This step reflects the idea of accumulation over an interval, not a single point. 3. Interpreting the Result The numerical value you obtain always represents a net accumulation: Positive value → net gain Negative value → net loss Zero → gains and losses balance The meaning depends entirely on the context of the rate: water volume, carbon exchange, energy transfer, population change. Units follow naturally: (rate units) × (input units) = accumulated units 4.7.8 A Simple Environmental Interpretation Suppose \(f(t)\) represents carbon flux (kg/hr). Then: \[ \int_a^b f(t)\,dt \] means: the net amount of carbon added to or removed from a system between times \(a\) and \(b\). Computing this as \(F(b) - F(a)\) is not skipping the accumulation process — it is using the mathematical structure of accumulation functions to compute it exactly. Worked Example: Applying the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Suppose the rate at which carbon is exchanged between an ecosystem and the atmosphere is modeled by: \[ f(t) = 3t^2 \] measured in kg of carbon per hour, where \(t\) is time in hours. We want to find the net carbon exchanged between \(t = 1\) hour and \(t = 4\) hours. 1. Identifying Antiderivatives To apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we first find an antiderivative \(F(t)\) such that: \[ F'(t) = f(t). \] Since: \[ f(t) = 3t^2, \] an antiderivative is: \[ F(t) = t^3, \] because: \[ \frac{d}{dt}(t^3) = 3t^2. \] 2. Evaluating at the Bounds Next, we evaluate the antiderivative at the upper and lower bounds. Upper bound: \[ F(4) = 4^3 = 64 \] Lower bound: \[ F(1) = 1^3 = 1 \] Subtract: \[ F(4) - F(1) = 64 - 1 = 63 \] So, \[ \int_1^4 3t^2\,dt = 63. \] 3. Interpreting the Result The value 63 represents the net accumulated carbon exchange over the interval from 1 to 4 hours. Because the result is positive, this means: there was a net gain of carbon by the ecosystem during this time. Including units: \[ (\text{kg/hr}) \times (\text{hr}) = \text{kg}, \] so the final answer is: \[ \boxed{63\ \text{kg of carbon}} \] Interpretation in Context This calculation does not tell us how fast carbon was moving at any single moment. It tells us how much carbon was transferred in total over a period of time. Even though the rate was changing continuously, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus allows us to compute the exact accumulated change using an antiderivative. The definite integral measures total change over an interval, not instantaneous behavior. 4.7.9 Critical Emphasis: More Than Plug-and-Chug It is tempting to treat \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) \] as a recipe: Find an antiderivative. Plug in numbers. Subtract. But without understanding why this works, it is easy to: lose track of units, misinterpret negative results, forget what is actually accumulating, or treat integrals as purely symbolic exercises. The formula works because integration and differentiation describe opposite sides of the same process: differentiation tracks instantaneous change, integration reconstructs total change from that information. 4.7.10 Key Takeaway The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part II) gives us an efficient way to compute accumulation — but its meaning comes from Part I. Definite integrals are not defined by antiderivatives. Antiderivatives are a powerful tool for computing definite integrals that already have a clear conceptual meaning. Understanding this connection allows you to compute integrals confidently and interpret them correctly in real environmental systems. Concept Check: Why Antiderivatives Form Families Why do antiderivatives differ by a constant? Click to reveal answer Adding a constant shifts a function vertically without changing its slope. Since derivatives depend only on slope, all such shifted functions share the same derivative — and so they’re all antiderivatives of the same rate. Concept Check: Why ‘Plug-and-Chug’ Is Dangerous Why is treating the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus as “plug-and-chug” dangerous? Click to reveal answer Without conceptual understanding, it’s easy to misinterpret signs, units, or meaning. A negative integral isn’t a calculation error — it’s information. The formula works because of accumulation logic, not algebraic coincidence; if you don’t see the accumulation, you’ll misread the result. Concept Check: Riemann Sums and FTC: Same Idea, Two Stages Why is it misleading to think of Riemann sums and definite integrals as separate formulas? Click to reveal answer They describe the same idea at different stages. Riemann sums show construction — how accumulation is assembled. The definite integral names the limiting result. Treating them as separate hides the fact that the FTC is just an efficient way to compute the limit. Concept Check: Perfect Measurement and the Integral How does refining a Riemann sum connect to the idea of “perfect measurement”? Click to reveal answer Refinement corresponds to measuring at infinitely fine resolution. The definite integral represents the total that would be obtained with no missing detail — the answer your gauge would give if it sampled continuously. Concept Check: Why Teach Riemann Sums First What is gained conceptually by teaching Riemann sums before antiderivatives? Click to reveal answer Students first understand what an integral represents and why it exists. Antiderivatives then appear as an efficient computational tool — not as the definition of integration. This protects against the misconception that an integral is “whatever \(F(b) - F(a)\) gives you”. 4.8 Practice Problems The problems in this section are designed to strengthen your calculation skills with definite integrals, especially using linearity, additivity, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. These are not concept checks — they are meant to feel like real calculus problems where careful setup and execution matter. Tips for Success Look for linearity first. If the integrand is a sum or has constants, split the integral before doing any computation. Factor out constants early. This simplifies both the antiderivative and the arithmetic. Watch the bounds carefully. Most errors come from evaluating \(F(b) - F(a)\) incorrectly, not from finding the antiderivative. Use additivity strategically. When information is given on subintervals, combine integrals rather than trying to invent a function. Keep units and interpretation in mind for applied problems — the final number should make sense in context. Work each problem symbolically, simplify as much as possible, and only then plug in the bounds. Check your result against the solution to catch small algebra or sign errors early. Problem 1 Evaluate the definite integral: \[ \int_0^2 \left(3x^2 + 4x\right)\,dx \] using linearity. Click to reveal solution Split using linearity: \[ \int_0^2 3x^2\,dx + \int_0^2 4x\,dx. \] Compute: \[ \int_0^2 3x^2\,dx = [x^3]_0^2 = 8, \quad \int_0^2 4x\,dx = [2x^2]_0^2 = 8. \] Add: \[ 8 + 8 = 16. \] \[ \boxed{16} \] Problem 2 Evaluate: \[ \int_1^3 5e^x\,dx. \] Click to reveal solution Factor out the constant: \[ 5\int_1^3 e^x\,dx. \] Antiderivative: \[ \int e^x\,dx = e^x. \] Evaluate: \[ 5(e^3 - e). \] \[ \boxed{5(e^3 - e)} \] Problem 3 Evaluate: \[ \int_{-1}^1 (2x - 3)\,dx. \] Click to reveal solution Antiderivative: \[ x^2 - 3x. \] Evaluate: \[ [x^2 - 3x]_{-1}^1 = (1 - 3) - (1 + 3) = -6. \] \[ \boxed{-6} \] Problem 4 Evaluate: \[ \int_0^1 (6x^3 - 4x + 2)\,dx. \] Click to reveal solution Apply linearity: \[ \int_0^1 6x^3\,dx - \int_0^1 4x\,dx + \int_0^1 2\,dx. \] Compute: \[ \frac{3}{2} - 2 + 2 = \frac{3}{2}. \] \[ \boxed{\tfrac{3}{2}} \] Problem 5 Suppose \[ \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx = 7 \quad \text{and} \quad \int_4^9 f(x)\,dx = -5. \] Find: \[ \int_0^9 f(x)\,dx. \] Click to reveal solution By additivity: \[ 7 + (-5) = 2. \] \[ \boxed{2} \] Problem 6 Evaluate: \[ \int_{-2}^2 3x^2\,dx. \] Click to reveal solution Antiderivative: \[ x^3. \] Evaluate: \[ [x^3]_{-2}^2 = 8 - (-8) = 16. \] \[ \boxed{16} \] Problem 7 Evaluate: \[ \int_0^{\pi} (4\sin x + 2)\,dx. \] Click to reveal solution Split: \[ 4\int_0^{\pi} \sin x\,dx + \int_0^{\pi} 2\,dx. \] Compute: \[ 4(2) + 2\pi = 8 + 2\pi. \] \[ \boxed{8 + 2\pi} \] Problem 8 Evaluate: \[ \int_1^2 (3x^2 - e^x)\,dx. \] Click to reveal solution Antiderivative: \[ x^3 - e^x. \] Evaluate: \[ (8 - e^2) - (1 - e) = 7 + e - e^2. \] \[ \boxed{7 + e - e^2} \] Problem 9 Evaluate: \[ \int_{-1}^{3} (2x - 1)\,dx \] by splitting the interval at \(x = 0\). Click to reveal solution Split: \[ \int_{-1}^{0} (2x - 1)\,dx + \int_0^{3} (2x - 1)\,dx. \] Antiderivative: \[ x^2 - x. \] Compute: \[ (-2) + 6 = 4. \] \[ \boxed{4} \] Problem 10 Evaluate: \[ \int_0^2 (5 - 3x)\,dx. \] Click to reveal solution Antiderivative: \[ 5x - \tfrac{3}{2}x^2. \] Evaluate: \[ (10 - 6) - 0 = 4. \] \[ \boxed{4} \] Problem 11 Suppose \[ \int_0^4 f(x)\,dx = 10 \quad \text{and} \quad \int_4^7 f(x)\,dx = -3. \] Find \[ \int_0^7 f(x)\,dx \] and interpret the result. Click to reveal solution By additivity, \[ \int_0^7 f(x)\,dx = 10 + (-3) = 7. \] This means there was a net gain of 7 units over the interval, despite some loss occurring. Problem 12 The rate at which nutrients enter a wetland is modeled by \[ f(t) = 4t \] measured in kg/day, where \(t\) is time in days. Find the net nutrient input between \(t = 2\) days and \(t = 5\) days. Click to reveal solution Step 1: Identify an antiderivative \[ F(t) = 2t^2 \] Step 2: Evaluate at the bounds \[ F(5) = 2(25) = 50 \] \[ F(2) = 2(4) = 8 \] Step 3: Subtract \[ F(5) - F(2) = 50 - 8 = 42 \] Interpretation: The wetland received a net input of 42 kg of nutrients over this time interval. Problem 13 The rate at which carbon is released from soil is given by \[ f(t) = 6e^t \] measured in kg/hr, where \(t\) is time in hours. Find the net carbon released between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 2\). Click to reveal solution Step 1: Identify an antiderivative \[ F(t) = 6e^t \] Step 2: Evaluate at the bounds \[ F(2) = 6e^2 \] \[ F(0) = 6e^0 = 6 \] Step 3: Subtract \[ 6e^2 - 6 \] Interpretation: This represents the net carbon released over the two-hour period, measured in kilograms. Problem 14 The rate of water uptake by vegetation is modeled by \[ f(t) = t^2 - 4 \] measured in liters/day, where \(t\) is time in days. Find the net water uptake from \(t = 1\) to \(t = 4\). Click to reveal solution Step 1: Identify an antiderivative \[ F(t) = \tfrac{1}{3}t^3 - 4t \] Step 2: Evaluate at the bounds \[ F(4) = \tfrac{64}{3} - 16 = \tfrac{16}{3} \] \[ F(1) = \tfrac{1}{3} - 4 = -\tfrac{11}{3} \] Step 3: Subtract \[ F(4) - F(1) = \tfrac{16}{3} - \left(-\tfrac{11}{3}\right) = 9 \] Interpretation: There was a net uptake of 9 liters of water over this interval. Problem 15 The rate at which energy is transferred across a surface is \[ f(t) = 5\sin t \] measured in J/s, where \(t\) is time in seconds. Find the net energy transferred from \(t = 0\) to \(t = \pi\). Click to reveal solution Step 1: Identify an antiderivative \[ F(t) = -5\cos t \] Step 2: Evaluate at the bounds \[ F(\pi) = -5(-1) = 5 \] \[ F(0) = -5(1) = -5 \] Step 3: Subtract \[ 5 - (-5) = 10 \] Interpretation: A total of 10 joules of energy were transferred over the interval. Problem 16 The rate of population change for a species is modeled by \[ f(t) = 12 - 3t \] measured in individuals/year, where \(t\) is time in years. Find the net population change between \(t = 1\) and \(t = 4\). Click to reveal solution Step 1: Identify an antiderivative \[ F(t) = 12t - \tfrac{3}{2}t^2 \] Step 2: Evaluate at the bounds \[ F(4) = 48 - 24 = 24 \] \[ F(1) = 12 - 1.5 = 10.5 \] Step 3: Subtract \[ 24 - 10.5 = 13.5 \] Interpretation: The population increased by 13.5 individuals over this time period. Problem 17: Total Streamflow Volume A flow gauge in a small drainage channel records the discharge rate \[ Q(t) = 3t^2 \quad \text{(L/min)}, \] where \(t\) is measured in minutes after the gauge began recording. Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, find the total volume of water that flowed through the gauge between \(t = 1\) and \(t = 4\) minutes. Click to reveal solution The total volume is \[ \int_1^4 3t^2\,dt. \] An antiderivative of \(3t^2\) is \(t^3\), so \[ \int_1^4 3t^2\,dt = \bigl[t^3\bigr]_1^4 = 64 - 1 = 63 \text{ L}. \] \[ \boxed{63 \text{ L of water flowed through the gauge.}} \] Problem 18: Net Carbon Exchange Over a Morning A flux tower over a young Douglas-fir stand records the net ecosystem carbon exchange rate during the first three hours after dawn as \[ F(t) = t^2 - 1 \quad \text{(mg C / m}^2\text{ / hr)}, \] with \(t\) measured in hours after dawn. Compute the net carbon exchange between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 3\) hours, and interpret the sign. Click to reveal solution Net carbon exchange: \[ \int_0^3 \bigl(t^2 - 1\bigr)\,dt = \left[\tfrac{t^3}{3} - t\right]_0^3 = \left(9 - 3\right) - 0 = 6 \text{ mg C / m}^2. \] Interpretation: The positive sign means the stand was a net carbon sink over the three-hour window — net uptake exceeded net release. Note that the rate was negative (a source) for the first hour (when \(t < 1\)) and positive (a sink) afterward, but the integrated total is positive: the sink phase outweighed the source phase. \[ \boxed{+6 \text{ mg C / m}^2\text{ (net uptake)}.} \] Problem 19: Pollutant Mass Loading to a Lake A regulator monitors the rate at which a contaminant enters a lake from a stormwater outfall during a four-hour storm: \[ L(t) = 4t \quad \text{(mg / s)}, \] with \(t\) measured in seconds since the start of monitoring. Find the total mass of contaminant delivered to the lake between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 60\) seconds. Click to reveal solution Total mass: \[ \int_0^{60} 4t \,dt = \bigl[2t^2\bigr]_0^{60} = 2(3600) - 0 = 7200 \text{ mg} = 7.2 \text{ g}. \] \[ \boxed{7.2 \text{ grams of contaminant entered the lake.}} \] For a regulator setting a maximum-daily-load standard, this is the kind of computation that turns a streaming sensor signal into a single defensible number. Problem 20: Net Population Change with a Sign-Changing Rate A fisheries biologist models the net daily change in a juvenile salmon population (immigration minus mortality) over a six-day window as \[ N'(t) = 6t - t^2 \quad \text{(fish/day)}, \] where \(t\) is days from the start of monitoring. Compute the net change in population between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 6\) days, and describe what the rate function says happens within that window. Click to reveal solution Net change: \[ \int_0^6 \bigl(6t - t^2\bigr)\,dt = \left[3t^2 - \tfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^6 = \left(108 - 72\right) - 0 = 36 \text{ fish}. \] What the rate says: \(N'(t) = 6t - t^2 = t(6 - t)\) is zero at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 6\), and positive between them. So the population grows continuously throughout the six-day window — but the rate of growth peaks around \(t = 3\) (where \(N'(t) = 9\) fish/day) and tapers back toward zero by day 6. The total net gain is 36 fish. \[ \boxed{+36 \text{ fish (net gain over the six-day window)}.} \]

Chapter 5 Techniques of Integration (Indefinite Integrals) The Fundamental Theorem turns any definite integral into “find an antiderivative, evaluate, subtract.” That only helps if you can find the antiderivative, and that’s where integration gets harder than differentiation. Differentiation has a recipe you can grind through. Integration doesn’t. What you build instead is pattern recognition: spotting when an integrand is a chain rule in disguise, a product, or a fraction that can be split apart. 5.1 Purpose of the Chapter Chapter 4 showed what a definite integral means and why antiderivatives compute it. This chapter is about how to find antiderivatives when they aren’t obvious. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to: compute indefinite integrals with the basic rules recognize when to use substitution, integration by parts or partial fractions connect each technique back to a derivative rule (chain rule, product rule) check your answer by differentiating it 5.2 Indefinite Integrals and the Constant of Integration A definite integral has bounds, and its answer is a number: the net change between \(a\) and \(b\). Take the bounds away and you’re asking a different question: which functions have this rate of change? A definite integral \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \] asks: how much changed between \(x=a\) and \(x=b\)? An indefinite integral \[ \int f(x)\,dx \] asks: which functions have derivative \(f(x)\)? Without bounds, the answer isn’t a number any more. It’s a function, and because there’s no starting point, it’s really a whole family of functions: \[ \int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C, \] where \(F'(x) = f(x)\). 5.2.1 Integrals as Families of Functions Consider the rate function: \[ f(x) = 2x. \] Any of the following functions has derivative \(2x\): \[ x^2,\quad x^2 + 3,\quad x^2 - 10,\quad x^2 + C. \] A derivative only describes slopes. All the curves on the right have the same slope at the same \(x\). They just start at different heights, and adding a constant doesn’t change a slope. That missing starting value is the constant \(C\). 5.2.2 Antiderivatives and the “+ C” An antiderivative of \(f(x)\) is any function whose derivative is \(f(x)\). Since the derivative of a constant is zero, \[  rac{d}{dx} ig(F(x) + C ig) = F'(x) + 0 = F'(x). \] So every antiderivative comes with a “+ C”. That isn’t a flaw. If \(f\) is a rate (carbon flux, inflow to a reservoir, population growth), the amount at any time depends on where you started: how much carbon was already there, how full the reservoir was, how big the population was. Different starting points give different curves with the same rate. The \(+C\) is how the math keeps track of that. Example: Two Lakes with the Same Inflow Two lakes get water at the same rate: \[ f(t) = 2t \quad 	ext{(m³/day)}, \] where \(t\) is time in days. Integrating gives \[ V(t) = t^2 + C, \] where \(V(t)\) is the volume in the lake and \(C\) is the volume at \(t = 0\). Lake A starts with 100 m³: \(V_A(t) = t^2 + 100\) Lake B starts with 250 m³: \(V_B(t) = t^2 + 250\) Same rate, so same shape. Different starting volumes, so one curve sits 150 m³ above the other. The rate sets the shape of the curve. The starting condition sets its height. 5.2.2.1 Leaving Out \(C\) Dropping the \(+C\) is the same as assuming the system started at zero. That’s rarely true unless the problem says so. 5.2.2.2 Why \(C\) Cancels in Definite Integrals In a definite integral the constant shows up twice and cancels: \[ (F(b) + C) - (F(a) + C) = F(b) - F(a). \] A definite integral measures change between two points, so the starting level doesn’t matter. An indefinite integral describes the amount itself, so it does. 5.2.2.3 Units Units still apply without bounds. If \(f(x)\) is in kg/day and \(x\) is in days, then \(\int f(x)\,dx\) is in kg. But without a starting value, you don’t know how many kg. You only know how the amount changes with \(x\). 5.2.2.4 Finding \(C\) from a Starting Value In real problems you find \(C\) from a known value. If the antiderivative is \(F(t) + C\) and the amount is \(A_0\) at time \(t_0\), solve \[ F(t_0) + C = A_0 \] for \(C\). That turns the family of curves into one specific model. 5.3 Reverse Differentiation as a Skill Most of the time in environmental work you know a rate (how fast a contaminant is decaying, how fast a stand is fixing carbon) and you want the amount. Getting from one to the other is antidifferentiation, and most of the rates you’ll meet come from a short list of functions. Every rule in this section is a derivative rule you already know, run backwards. The skill isn’t memorizing formulas. It’s looking at an integrand and recognizing it as the derivative of something familiar. 5.3.1 The “Antiderivative Dictionary” Think of it as a dictionary. When you integrate, you’re asking: have I seen this as a derivative before? These are the entries to know cold. 5.3.1.1 Power Rule (in Reverse) From differentiation: \[  rac{d}{dx}(x^n) = nx^{n-1} \] Reversing this: \[ \int x^n \, dx =  rac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \quad (n 
eq -1) \] Examples \[ \int x^4 dx =  rac{x^5}{5} + C \] \[ \int x^{-3} dx =  rac{x^{-2}}{-2} + C = - rac{1}{2x^2} + C \] 5.3.1.2 The Special Case: \(x^{-1}\) The power rule fails when \(n = -1\). Instead: \[ \int  rac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C \] It comes straight from: \[  rac{d}{dx}(\ln|x|) =  rac{1}{x} \] Key recognition trigger: Any time you see a lone \(1/x\), think logarithm. 5.3.1.3 Exponentials and Logarithms Exponentials are special because they reproduce themselves under differentiation. \[  rac{d}{dx}(e^x) = e^x \] So: \[ \int e^x dx = e^x + C \] Similarly: \[ \int a^x dx =  rac{a^x}{\ln a} + C \quad (a > 0, a 
eq 1) \] 5.3.1.4 Basic Trigonometric Antiderivatives These come directly from familiar derivative rules. Integrand Antiderivative \(\cos x\) \(\sin x + C\) \(\sin x\) \(-\cos x + C\) \(\sec^2 x\) \(	an x + C\) \(\csc^2 x\) \(-\cot x + C\) \(\sec x 	an x\) \(\sec x + C\) \(\csc x \cot x\) \(-\csc x + C\) Sign matters. For sine and cosine in particular, the negative sign is part of the recognition. 5.3.2 Pattern Recognition Over Memorization Integration is less about remembering formulas than about recognizing them: Look at the integrand. Ask what derivative it looks like. Match the structure, not the symbols. Apply the matching reverse rule. 5.3.2.1 Reading an Integrand as a Derivative Take \[ \int 6x^5 dx. \] Instead of “apply the power rule,” ask: what has derivative \(6x^5\)? You know \( rac{d}{dx}(x^6) = 6x^5\), so \[ \int 6x^5 dx = x^6 + C. \] That habit matters more as the functions get more complicated. 5.3.2.2 Quick Recognition Cues Powers of \(x\) → power rule \(1/x\) → logarithm \(e^x\) → exponential A trig function on its own → basic trig antiderivative A constant in front → pull it out If nothing jumps out, that’s not a failure. It usually means you need one of the techniques coming up next. Concept Check: Why Integration Is Harder Than Differentiation Differentiation has a step-by-step recipe: power rule, chain rule, product rule, and you can grind through anything. Integration doesn’t work that way. Why? Click to reveal answer Differentiation is mechanical: every elementary function has a derivative you can build from a few rules. Integration runs the other way. You’re looking for a function with a given derivative, and there’s no recipe that always works. Some innocent-looking integrands, like \(e^{-x^2}\) or \(\sin(x)/x\), don’t have an antiderivative you can write with elementary functions at all. So integration is a set of techniques you try, check and sometimes abandon. Concept Check: Reading an Integrand as a Derivative When you spot \(\int 2x\cos(x^2)\,dx\) and immediately think “that’s a chain-rule derivative in disguise”, what specifically are you noticing? Click to reveal answer One factor, \(2x\), is exactly the derivative of the inside of the other factor, the \(x^2\) inside the cosine. Differentiating \(\sin(x^2)\) with the chain rule gives \(\cos(x^2)\cdot 2x\), which is your integrand. So an antiderivative is \(\sin(x^2) + C\). The thing to look for: an inner function and its derivative, both present. 5.4 Substitution: When a Function Is Hiding Inside Another Substitution handles composite rates: a rate that depends on something that’s itself changing. A reaction rate that depends on concentration, which depends on time. An oxygen-uptake rate that depends on temperature, which depends on depth. Integrals like these are hard because they’re nested, not because they’re complicated. Substitution lets you deal with the inside first. It’s the chain rule in reverse. 5.4.1 The Big Idea: The Chain Rule in Reverse The chain rule says \[  rac{d}{dx} ig(F(g(x)) ig) = F'(g(x))\,g'(x). \] So substitution works when the integrand looks like \[ f(g(x))\,g'(x), \] where \(f\) is the derivative of some outer function \(F\). The question to ask: Do I see a function inside another function, along with (almost) its derivative? That’s hard to spot at first. It gets easier with practice. Just as important is recognizing when substitution isn’t working, and what that tells you to try instead. 5.4.1.1 Recognizing \(f(g(x))g'(x)\) Consider: \[ \int (3x^2 + 1)^5 \cdot 6x \, dx. \] Read it structurally: Inner function: \(g(x) = 3x^2 + 1\) Outer function: \(F(u) = u^5\) Derivative of the inner function: \(g'(x) = 6x\) This matches the chain rule pattern exactly. Instead of expanding the fifth power, rename the inner function and the integral gets simple. 5.4.1.2 Why It’s a Change of Variable, Not a Trick Substitution can feel like a trick when it’s taught as a procedure. It isn’t. You change variables so the integral matches something you already know how to do. The math is the same. Only the variable you’re measuring in changes, the same way you might re-express time-series data in terms of temperature if temperature is what drives the process. 5.4.2 The Mechanics of \(u\)-Substitution Once the structure is recognized, the mechanics follow a consistent pattern. 5.4.2.1 Step 1: Choose \(u\) Choose \(u\) to be the inner function. Example: \[ \int (3x^2 + 1)^5 \cdot 6x \, dx \] Let: \[ u = 3x^2 + 1. \] 5.4.2.2 Step 2: Convert \(dx\) to \(du\) Differentiate \(u\): \[  rac{du}{dx} = 6x \quad \Rightarrow \quad du = 6x\,dx. \] This step matters more than it looks. 5.4.2.2.1 What \(dx\) Means An integral starts as a Riemann sum, \[ \sum f(x_i)\,\Delta x, \] where \(f(x_i)\) is the height of each rectangle and \(\Delta x\) is its width. As the widths shrink, the sum becomes \(\int f(x)\,dx\). So \(dx\) is a very thin width measured in \(x\). When you switch to \(u\), you’re measuring in \(u\) instead. The heights get rewritten in terms of \(u\), and so do the widths. Leave \(dx\) behind and you’re mixing two different rulers. \(du = 6x\,dx\) tells you how a small step in \(x\) translates into a small step in \(u\). The factor \(6x\) is the conversion between the two rulers. Forget to convert the differential and the integral no longer means what it did. 5.4.2.3 Step 3: Rewrite the Integral in Terms of \(u\) Substitute: \((3x^2 + 1) ightarrow u\) \(6x\,dx ightarrow du\) The integral becomes: \[ \int u^5 \, du. \] Now the structure is simple. 5.4.2.4 Step 4: Integrate and Substitute Back Integrate: \[ \int u^5 du =  rac{u^6}{6} + C. \] Substitute back: \[  rac{(3x^2 + 1)^6}{6} + C. \] 5.4.3 Why Substitution Works You’ve turned a composite rate into a simple one by measuring it in terms of the inner quantity first, then translating back to the original variable. 5.4.4 Substitution in Definite Integrals Substitution works the same way in definite integrals, with one shortcut: you can change the bounds instead of substituting back. 5.4.4.1 Changing the Bounds Example: \[ \int_0^2 (3x^2 + 1)^5 \cdot 6x \, dx \] Let: \[ u = 3x^2 + 1. \] Convert the bounds: When \(x = 0\): \(u = 1\) When \(x = 2\): \(u = 13\) Now the integral becomes: \[ \int_1^{13} u^5 \, du. \] Changing the bounds means you never have to switch back to \(x\), so there’s less algebra and fewer chances to drop a constant or a sign. Worked Example: Converting the Differential Evaluate: \[ \int 2x \, e^{x^2} \, dx \] Step 1: Recognize the Structure Inner function: \(x^2\) Outer function: \(F(u) = e^u\) Derivative of the inner function: \(2x\) This matches the chain rule pattern. Step 2: Choose \(u\) Let: \[ u = x^2. \] Then: \[ du = 2x\,dx. \] The whole factor \(2x\,dx\) is exactly \(du\). Step 3: Rewrite the Integral in Terms of \(u\) \[ \int e^{u}\,du. \] Step 4: Integrate and Substitute Back \[ e^{x^2} + C. \] The function and the width both have to be written in the same variable. 5.4.5 Common Pitfalls Most substitution mistakes are one of these. 5.4.5.1 Missing the Derivative Factor \[ \int (x^2 + 1)^4 dx \] There’s no \(2x\) here, so substitution won’t simplify it. (Expanding the power and using the power rule will.) 5.4.5.2 Writing \(du\) Without the \(dx\) \[ u = x^2 + 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad du = 2x \] is incomplete. It should be \(du = 2x\,dx\). 5.4.5.3 Switching Back Too Early Once the integral is in terms of \(u\), stay in \(u\) until you’ve integrated. 5.4.6 Before You Substitute Is there a function inside another function? Is the derivative of the inside present, up to a constant? Will the substitution make the integral simpler? If the answer is no, that’s useful. It tells you to try something else. 5.4.7 When the Derivative Is Almost There – Close Enough Can Be Enough Often the derivative of the inner function is there up to a constant. That’s fine. 5.4.7.1 Example Evaluate: \[ \int (3x^2 + 1)^4 \cdot x \, dx \] 5.4.7.2 Step 1: Recognize the Structure Inner function: \(3x^2 + 1\) Derivative: \(6x\) The integrand contains \(x\), not \(6x\). 5.4.7.3 Step 2: Adjust with a Constant \[ = \int (3x^2 + 1)^4 \cdot  rac{1}{6}(6x)\, dx =  rac{1}{6} \int (3x^2 + 1)^4 \cdot 6x\, dx. \] 5.4.7.4 Step 3: Substitute and Integrate \[  rac{1}{6} \int u^4 du =  rac{(3x^2 + 1)^5}{30} + C. \] 5.4.8 Course Correct A constant mismatch is fine. A mismatch that depends on \(x\) means substitution is the wrong tool. Concept Check: Spotting When Substitution Is the Right Move What two features must an integrand have for substitution to work cleanly? Click to reveal answer An inner function: some \(g(x)\) wrapped inside another function, like the \(x^2\) inside \(\cos(x^2)\) or the \(3x^2 + 1\) inside \((\,\cdot\,)^5\). Its derivative: \(g'(x)\) is in the integrand as a factor, possibly times a constant. With both, \(u = g(x)\) collapses the integral into something simple. If the derivative is missing altogether, not just off by a constant, substitution won’t help. Concept Check: Why dx Must Become du, Not Just Disappear When you do a substitution, why isn’t it enough to just rename \(x\) to \(u\) inside the function? Why does \(dx\) also have to be converted to \(du\)? Click to reveal answer Because \(dx\) and \(du\) measure widths in different units. \(\int f(x)\,dx\) is a limit of Riemann sums \(\sum f(x_i)\,\Delta x\), where each width is measured in \(x\). Switch to \(u\) and the widths are measured in \(u\), and in general \(\Delta u 
eq \Delta x\). The relationship \(du = g'(x)\,dx\) is the conversion. Skip it and you’re adding heights in one unit times widths in another, which gives the wrong total. 5.5 Integration by Parts: When Accumulation Involves a Product Integration by parts is for products of two functions where one of them gets simpler when you differentiate it. In environmental work that comes up when the rate is itself a product of two changing factors, like a respiration rate that rises with time but decays as the substrate runs out. Substitution handles nesting. Integration by parts handles products. It’s the product rule, rearranged. 5.5.1 The Big Idea: The Product Rule in Reverse The product rule says \[  rac{d}{dx} ig(u(x)v(x) ig) = u'(x)v(x) + u(x)v'(x). \] Rearrange to isolate one of the terms: \[ u(x)v'(x) =  rac{d}{dx} ig(u(x)v(x) ig) - u'(x)v(x). \] Integrate both sides: \[ \int u(x)v'(x)\,dx = u(x)v(x) - \int u'(x)v(x)\,dx. \] That’s integration by parts, usually written \[ \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du. \] 5.5.2 What the Formula Does It doesn’t evaluate the integral for you. It moves the difficulty. You differentiate one factor (which, if you chose well, simplifies it) and integrate the other. If the integral that’s left is easier than the one you started with, it worked. If not, try a different choice or a different method. 5.5.3 When Integration by Parts Is the Right Tool Use it when the integrand is a product, and differentiating one factor makes it simpler. Common cases: a polynomial times an exponential or a trig function a logarithm times anything an inverse trig function times a power of \(x\) The question to ask: if I differentiate one factor, does it get simpler? Quick Check: \(\int x \sin x \, dx\) Differentiate \(x\) and you get \(1\). Simpler. Differentiate \(\sin x\) and you get \(\cos x\). No simpler. So choose \(u = x\). Choose the other way round and you’re still left with a product of two non-trivial functions. That’s your warning sign. “Simpler” doesn’t mean finished. It means less structure than before. 5.5.4 Choosing \(u\) and \(dv\) The method requires a choice: one part becomes \(u\), the other becomes \(dv\). There is no single correct rule, but a common guideline is: Choose \(u\) to be the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated. Often, but not always, that means: logarithms, inverse trig functions, algebraic powers of \(x\). 5.5.5 A First Worked Example Evaluate: \[ \int x e^x \, dx. \] 5.5.5.1 Step 1: Choose \(u\) and \(dv\) Let: \[ u = x. \] Take the derivative of both sides with respect to \(x\): \[  rac{du}{dx} =  rac{d}{dx}(x) = 1. \] Multiply both sides by \(dx\): \[ du = dx. \] Now let the rest of the integrand be \(dv\): \[ dv = e^x\,dx. \] Integrate to find \(v\): \[ v = \int e^x\,dx = e^x. \] So \(u\) is the factor you differentiate (giving \(du\)) and \(dv\) is the factor you integrate (giving \(v\)). 5.5.5.2 Step 2: Apply the Formula \[ \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du \] \[ \int x e^x dx = x e^x - \int e^x dx. \] 5.5.5.3 Step 3: Finish the Integral \[ x e^x - e^x + C. \] Or factor: \[ e^x(x - 1) + C. \] 5.5.6 Why This Worked Differentiating \(x\) turned it into a constant. Integrating \(e^x\) left it unchanged. The integral that was left, \(\int e^x\,dx\), was easier than the one you started with. That’s the whole goal. 5.5.7 A Second Example: Logarithms Evaluate: \[ \int \ln x \, dx. \] There’s no obvious product here, and no inner function either. The trick is to see it as a product with 1: \[ \ln x = (\ln x)\cdot 1. \] 5.5.7.1 Step 1: Choose \(u\) and \(dv\) Let: \[ u = \ln x \quad \Rightarrow \quad du =  rac{1}{x} dx. \] Let: \[ dv = dx \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = x. \] 5.5.7.2 Step 2: Apply the Formula \[ \int \ln x \, dx = x\ln x - \int x \cdot  rac{1}{x} dx. \] 5.5.7.3 Step 3: Simplify \[ x\ln x - \int 1\,dx = x\ln x - x + C. \] 5.5.8 Common Pitfalls 5.5.8.1 Choosing a \(u\) That Doesn’t Simplify For \(\int x e^x dx\), choosing \(u = e^x\) gets you nowhere: its derivative is still \(e^x\). Pick the factor that simplifies. 5.5.8.2 Losing the Minus Sign \[ \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du. \] The minus sign is the most common source of errors. 5.5.8.3 Stopping Too Soon Sometimes you have to apply it more than once. For \[ \int x^2 e^x dx, \] each round knocks the power of \(x\) down by one until the integral is easy. 5.5.9 Before You Use Integration by Parts Is the integrand a product? Does differentiating one factor make it simpler? Have you ruled out substitution? Concept Check: Choosing u and dv in Integration by Parts When you apply integration by parts to \(\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du\), how should you decide which factor is \(u\) and which is \(dv\)? Click to reveal answer Pick \(u\) to be the factor that gets simpler when you differentiate it. Polynomials shrink (\(x^2 	o 2x 	o 2 	o 0\)). Logarithms and inverse trig functions turn into algebraic fractions (\(\ln x 	o 1/x\)). Those make good \(u\)’s. The other factor is \(dv\), and you need to be able to integrate it. Exponentials and basic trig functions are good \(dv\)’s because integrating them doesn’t make them worse. If you like mnemonics: LIATE (Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). Earlier in the list usually means \(u\). Concept Check: Why Integration by Parts Works What’s the connection between integration by parts and the product rule for derivatives? Click to reveal answer It is the product rule, integrated. Start with \( rac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'\) and integrate both sides: \[ uv = \int u'v\,dx + \int uv'\,dx. \] Rearrange: \[ \int uv'\,dx = uv - \int u'v\,dx, \] which is \(\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du\). Substitution is the chain rule run backwards. Integration by parts is the product rule run backwards. 5.6 Partial Fractions: When a Rational Function Can Be Taken Apart Some important environmental rate equations, like logistic growth and Michaelis–Menten kinetics, turn into rational functions (a polynomial over a polynomial) when you try to integrate them. Partial fractions splits a rational function into simple pieces you already know how to integrate. Substitution is for nesting, and integration by parts is for products. Partial fractions is for ratios of polynomials: \[  rac{P(x)}{Q(x)}. \] 5.6.1 Split It, Then Integrate The hard part here is algebra, not calculus. Instead of integrating a complicated fraction, ask: can I rewrite it as a sum of simple fractions? If so, integrate each one, because integration is linear: \[ \int (f(x) + g(x))\,dx = \int f(x)\,dx + \int g(x)\,dx. \] The pieces you’re aiming for look like \[  rac{A}{x - a}, \] because you already know \[ \int  rac{1}{x - a}\,dx = \ln|x - a| + C. \] It can feel like you’re making the problem bigger by splitting one fraction into several. You’re not. You’re turning one fraction you can’t integrate into several you can. 5.6.2 When to Use It the integrand is a rational function the numerator’s degree is less than the denominator’s (or you can make it so) the denominator factors 5.6.3 Step 0: Make the Fraction Proper Check the degrees first. If \[ \deg(P) \ge \deg(Q), \] do polynomial division first. For example, \[  rac{x^2 + 1}{x - 1} = x + 1 +  rac{2}{x - 1}. \] Only the leftover fraction needs partial fractions. 5.6.4 The Denominator Sets the Form Each factor in the denominator gets its own term. For example, \[ (x - 1)(x + 2) \] gives \[  rac{A}{x - 1} +  rac{B}{x + 2}. \] \(A\) and \(B\) are whatever constants make the algebra work. 5.6.5 Case 1: Distinct Linear Factors Consider: \[ \int  rac{5x + 1}{(x - 1)(x + 2)}\,dx. \] Because the denominator factors into distinct linear terms, we write: \[  rac{5x + 1}{(x - 1)(x + 2)} =  rac{A}{x - 1} +  rac{B}{x + 2}. \] The goal is to find constants \(A\) and \(B\). 5.6.5.1 Solving for the Coefficients Start with the decomposition: \[  rac{5x + 1}{(x - 1)(x + 2)} =  rac{A}{x - 1} +  rac{B}{x + 2}. \] Multiply both sides by the common denominator \((x - 1)(x + 2)\): \[ 5x + 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1). \] Expand the right-hand side: \[ 5x + 1 = Ax + 2A + Bx - B. \] Combine like terms: \[ 5x + 1 = (A + B)x + (2A - B). \] Match coefficients: Coefficient of \(x\): \[ A + B = 5 \] Constant term: \[ 2A - B = 1 \] Solve the system. Add the equations: \[ (A + B) + (2A - B) = 5 + 1 \] \[ 3A = 6 \] \[ A = 2. \] Substitute into \(A + B = 5\): \[ 2 + B = 5 \] \[ B = 3. \] So the coefficients are: \[ A = 2, \quad B = 3. \] 5.6.5.2 Integrate Term by Term Once the decomposition is complete, the integral becomes a sum of simpler integrals: \[ \int \left( rac{2}{x - 1} +  rac{3}{x + 2}ight)\,dx. \] Use linearity to split the integral: \[ \int \left( rac{2}{x - 1} +  rac{3}{x + 2}ight)\,dx = \int  rac{2}{x - 1}\,dx + \int  rac{3}{x + 2}\,dx. \] Now pull constants outside each integral: \[ \int  rac{2}{x - 1}\,dx + \int  rac{3}{x + 2}\,dx = 2\int  rac{1}{x - 1}\,dx + 3\int  rac{1}{x + 2}\,dx. \] Use the logarithm antiderivative identity: \[ \int  rac{1}{x-a}\,dx = \ln|x-a| + C. \] Apply it to each term: For \(a=1\): \[ 2\int  rac{1}{x - 1}\,dx = 2\ln|x - 1|. \] For \(a=-2\): \[ 3\int  rac{1}{x + 2}\,dx = 3\ln|x + 2|. \] Combine the results: \[ 2\ln|x - 1| + 3\ln|x + 2| + C. \] The single constant \(C\) at the end accounts for the constants that would arise from each integral. 5.6.6 Case 2: Repeated Linear Factors If the denominator contains a repeated linear factor such as \[ (x - a)^2, \] then each power of that factor requires its own term in the decomposition. This ensures that the decomposition has enough flexibility to match the original numerator. 5.6.6.1 Example Evaluate: \[ \int  rac{2x + 3}{(x - 1)^2}\,dx. \] This example is deliberately chosen so that both terms in the decomposition matter. 5.6.6.2 Step 1: Write the Partial Fraction Decomposition Because the factor \((x - 1)\) appears with power 2, we must include one term for each power: \[  rac{2x + 3}{(x - 1)^2} =  rac{A}{x - 1} +  rac{B}{(x - 1)^2}. \] The goal is to determine the constants \(A\) and \(B\). 5.6.6.3 Step 2: Clear the Denominator Multiply both sides by \((x - 1)^2\): \[ 2x + 3 = A(x - 1) + B. \] This equation must hold for all values of \(x\). 5.6.6.4 Step 3: Choose a Convenient Value of \(x\) Because the equation is true for all \(x\), we can choose values that simplify the algebra. 5.6.6.4.1 Why Choose \(x = 1\)? Substituting \(x = 1\) eliminates the term involving \(A\): \[ 2(1) + 3 = A(1 - 1) + B. \] So: \[ 5 = 0 + B, \] which gives \[ B = 5. \] This isolates one coefficient immediately. 5.6.6.5 Step 4: Solve for the Remaining Coefficient Substitute \(B = 5\) back into the equation: \[ 2x + 3 = A(x - 1) + 5. \] Subtract 5 from both sides: \[ 2x - 2 = A(x - 1). \] Factor the left-hand side: \[ 2(x - 1) = A(x - 1). \] Since this must hold for all \(x 
eq 1\), we conclude: \[ A = 2. \] 5.6.6.6 Step 5: Write the Final Decomposition \[  rac{2x + 3}{(x - 1)^2} =  rac{2}{x - 1} +  rac{5}{(x - 1)^2}. \] This is the key payoff of partial fractions: a single complicated ratio rewritten as a sum of simpler pieces. 5.6.6.7 Step 6: Integrate Term by Term Split the integral: \[ \int \left( rac{2}{x - 1} +  rac{5}{(x - 1)^2}ight)dx. \] Integrate each term separately: \[ \int  rac{2}{x - 1}dx = 2\ln|x - 1| \] \[ \int  rac{5}{(x - 1)^2}dx = 5\int (x - 1)^{-2}dx = - rac{5}{x - 1}. \] Combine the results: \[ 2\ln|x - 1| -  rac{5}{x - 1} + C. \] 5.6.7 Repeated Factors Every power of a repeated factor needs its own term. Without them, the algebra can’t reproduce the numerator. Repeated factors give both a logarithm and a power-rule term. Plugging in the \(x\) that zeroes a factor is the fastest way to find a coefficient. Rewrite first. Integrate second. 5.6.8 Common Pitfalls Skipping polynomial division. If the fraction isn’t proper, the decomposition fails or gets messy. Divide first. Missing terms. Every factor and every power needs a term. For example, \[ (x - 1)^3 \Rightarrow  rac{A}{x - 1} +  rac{B}{(x - 1)^2} +  rac{C}{(x - 1)^3}. \] Losing sight of the goal. Finding \(A\) and \(B\) isn’t the point. The point is pieces you can integrate. 5.6.9 Before You Use Partial Fractions Is it a rational function? Is the fraction proper, or can you make it proper? Does the denominator factor? Concept Check: Recognizing When Partial Fractions Is the Right Tool You see an integral \(\int  rac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\,dx\) where both \(P\) and \(Q\) are polynomials. What signals tell you partial fractions is the right move (versus substitution or something else)? Click to reveal answer When all three are true: The integrand is a ratio of polynomials. The numerator’s degree is less than the denominator’s (if not, divide first). There’s no obvious substitution. If the derivative of the denominator is sitting in the numerator, use substitution instead, since \(\int Q'(x)/Q(x)\,dx = \ln|Q(x)| + C\). Then factor the denominator, decompose, and integrate each piece. Concept Check: Why the Decomposition Depends on the Denominator’s Factors When you decompose a rational function into partial fractions, why does the form of the decomposition depend on what kind of factors are in the denominator (distinct linear, repeated linear, irreducible quadratic)? Click to reveal answer Because each kind of factor needs a different kind of piece to integrate: A distinct linear factor \((x - a)\) gets \( rac{A}{x-a}\), which integrates to a logarithm. A repeated linear factor \((x - a)^2\) needs both \( rac{A}{x-a}\) and \( rac{B}{(x-a)^2}\). The second integrates to \(-1/(x-a)\), a different shape, and you need both shapes to rebuild the numerator. An irreducible quadratic \((x^2 + bx + c)\) needs a numerator \(Ax + B\), which integrates to a mix of \(\ln\) and \(\arctan\). (That case is beyond what we’ll test in this course.) Each piece is chosen so that it lands on something in the dictionary. 5.7 Strategy: How to Choose a Method You now have several techniques. The hard part is no longer how to do each one, but which one to try first. Pause before you compute. 5.7.1 What to Try, in Order Simplify. Expand, cancel, split sums, pull out constants. A lot of “hard” integrals turn easy after a tidy-up. Basic rules. Power rule, exponentials, logarithms, basic trig, linearity. If the integrand is already a sum of familiar pieces, you’re done. Substitution. Is there a function inside another function, with (almost) its derivative? Look for powers of expressions like \((3x^2+1)^5\), exponentials like \(e^{x^2}\), and fractions where the numerator looks like the derivative of the denominator. Integration by parts. Is it a product where one factor gets simpler when differentiated? Think \(x e^x\), \(x \sin x\), \(\ln x\). Partial fractions. Is it a ratio of polynomials with a denominator that factors (after division, if needed)? None of the above. Some integrals have no antiderivative you can write down. Then you approximate numerically (Chapter 6). Recognizing that is a skill too. Trying a method and backing out isn’t failure. If substitution makes the integral messier, or parts makes it more complicated, that tells you something about the structure. 5.7.2 Habits That Catch Mistakes Check by differentiating. Differentiate your answer. If you don’t get the integrand back, something’s wrong. It’s the fastest way to catch sign errors and dropped constants. Check units and sign in applied problems. Positive rates should make the total go up. Negative rates should bring it down. A correct-looking answer with the wrong units or sign is still wrong. Concept Check: Always Try to Rewrite First Before reaching for substitution, IBP, or partial fractions, what should always be your first step on an integral that doesn’t look obvious? Click to reveal answer Rewrite and simplify. Distribute products, split fractions, separate sums, cancel common factors, pull constants out front. A lot of “hard” integrals turn into basic rules once you tidy up the integrand. Reaching for a heavy technique on an integrand you haven’t simplified usually makes things worse. Concept Check: Why Differentiation Is the Strongest Check After computing an indefinite integral, why is differentiating your answer the strongest way to check it, stronger than redoing the integration? Click to reveal answer Because differentiation is mechanical. If you differentiate your answer \(F(x)\) and don’t get back exactly \(f(x)\), something is definitely wrong. Redoing the integration can repeat the same mistake. Differentiating the result checks it independently, using different steps. 5.8 Practice 5.8.1 Practice: Fast Recognition Drills These are about speed. Practice spotting the pattern before you compute. Learn the vocabulary before writing sentences. 5.8.2 Practice: Substitution (u-Sub) Pattern Recognition and Application Slow down here. See the structure first, then do the mechanics. Part A: Identifying the Parts of the Integral (Pattern Recognition) For each integrand below: Identify the inner function (if there is one). Identify the derivative of the inner function. Decide whether substitution is appropriate. Check whether the derivative is present exactly, off by a constant, or missing. Do not compute the integral yet. A Helpful Instruction: “Off by a Constant” Is Still OK The derivative of the inner function doesn’t have to appear exactly. If the integrand has \[ g'(x)\quad 	ext{or} \quad c\,g'(x), \] where \(c\) is a constant, substitution still works: factor out the constant and carry on. What doesn’t work is a mismatch that depends on \(x\). Warning: Some of These Aren’t Substitution Problems The list mixes problems where substitution works with problems where it doesn’t. Tell them apart before you compute. A1. \[ \int (3x^2 + 1)^5 \cdot 6x \, dx \] A2. \[ \int (x^2 + 1)^4 \, dx \] A3. \[ \int e^{x^2} \cdot 2x \, dx \] A4. \[ \int x e^{x} \, dx \] A5. \[ \int  rac{4x}{x^2 + 7} \, dx \] A6. \[ \int \cos(5x)\, dx \] A7. \[ \int (x + 1)^4 \, dx \] Click to reveal analysis A1 Inner function: \(3x^2 + 1\) Derivative: \(6x\) Match: exact Substitution: yes A2 Inner function: \(x^2 + 1\) Derivative: \(2x\) Match: missing Substitution: no Reason: no factor of \(x\) to supply \(du\) A3 Inner function: \(x^2\) Derivative: \(2x\) Match: exact Substitution: yes A4 Structure: product, not nesting Substitution: no Reason: derivative mismatch depends on \(x\); integration by parts is appropriate A5 Inner function: \(x^2 + 7\) Derivative: \(2x\) Match: off by a constant Substitution: yes A6 Inner function: \(5x\) Derivative: \(5\) Match: off by a constant Substitution: yes A7 Inner function: \(x + 1\) Derivative: \(1\) Match: exact Substitution: yes (the basic power rule also works) Part B: Solve Using Substitution Now compute each integral where substitution is appropriate. If substitution is not appropriate, do not force it. B1. \[ \int (3x^2 + 1)^5 \cdot 6x \, dx \] B2. \[ \int e^{x^2} \cdot 2x \, dx \] B3. \[ \int  rac{4x}{x^2 + 7} \, dx \] B4. \[ \int \cos(5x)\, dx \] B5. \[ \int (x + 1)^4 \, dx \] Click to reveal solutions B1 Let \(u = 3x^2 + 1\), \(du = 6x\,dx\) \[  rac{(3x^2 + 1)^6}{6} + C \] B2 Let \(u = x^2\), \(du = 2x\,dx\) \[ e^{x^2} + C \] B3 Let \(u = x^2 + 7\), \(du = 2x\,dx\) \[ 2\ln(x^2 + 7) + C \] B4 Let \(u = 5x\), \(du = 5\,dx\) \[  rac{1}{5}\sin(5x) + C \] B5 Let \(u = x + 1\), \(du = dx\) \[  rac{(x + 1)^5}{5} + C \] Reflection Prompt Did you find the inner function before choosing \(u\)? Did you check whether the derivative was exact, off by a constant, or missing? Did you reject substitution when it didn’t fit? Being able to say “this isn’t a substitution problem” is as important as doing substitution. 5.8.3 Practice: Integration by Parts (Pattern Recognition and Application) This set is about deciding when integration by parts fits, then doing it carefully. Part A: Identifying the Structure For each integrand below: Is it a product? If you differentiate one factor, does it get simpler? Is integration by parts the right tool? If so, choose \(u\) and \(dv\). Don’t compute yet. What “Simpler” Means A factor gets simpler if differentiating it lowers its degree, removes structure (a polynomial becoming a constant), or turns something complicated into something basic. If differentiating keeps it just as complex, or makes it worse, that’s a bad sign. Warning: Not Every Product Needs Integration by Parts Some products are easier with substitution, the basic rules or a bit of algebra. This list mixes both kinds. A1. \[ \int x e^x \, dx \] A2. \[ \int x \sin x \, dx \] A3. \[ \int e^{x^2} \cdot 2x \, dx \] A4. \[ \int \ln x \, dx \] A5. \[ \int (x + 1)^4 \, dx \] A6. \[ \int x^2 e^x \, dx \] Click to reveal analysis A1 Product: yes Simplifies when differentiating \(x\) Method: integration by parts Good choice: \(u = x\), \(dv = e^x dx\) A2 Product: yes Simplifies when differentiating \(x\) Method: integration by parts Good choice: \(u = x\), \(dv = \sin x dx\) A3 Product: yes Better structure: nesting Method: substitution Reason: derivative matches inner function A4 Product: implicit (\(\ln x \cdot 1\)) Simplifies when differentiating \(\ln x\) Method: integration by parts Good choice: \(u = \ln x\), \(dv = dx\) A5 Not a meaningful product Method: basic power rule Reason: no simplification via differentiation A6 Product: yes Simplifies when differentiating \(x^2\) Method: integration by parts (possibly repeated) Part B: Solve Using Integration by Parts Now compute each integral where integration by parts is appropriate. Write your choices of \(u\) and \(dv\) clearly before applying the formula. B1. \[ \int x e^x \, dx \] B2. \[ \int x \sin x \, dx \] B3. \[ \int \ln x \, dx \] B4. \[ \int x^2 e^x \, dx \] Click to reveal solutions B1 Let \(u = x\), \(dv = e^x dx\) \[ x e^x - e^x + C \] B2 Let \(u = x\), \(dv = \sin x dx\) \[ -x \cos x + \sin x + C \] B3 Let \(u = \ln x\), \(dv = dx\) \[ x \ln x - x + C \] B4 Let \(u = x^2\), \(dv = e^x dx\) Apply integration by parts twice: \[ x^2 e^x - 2x e^x + 2e^x + C \] Reflection Prompt Did you check it was a product before choosing integration by parts? Did differentiating \(u\) actually simplify things? If it didn’t work, did that point you to a better method? 5.8.4 Practice: Partial Fractions (Structured Practice) Two problems of each type, with the key algebra steps shown. For each problem: 1. Set up the decomposition. 2. Solve for the coefficients. 3. Integrate term by term. Type I: Distinct Linear Factors P1.1 \[ \int  rac{3x + 5}{(x + 1)(x + 2)}\,dx \] P1.2 \[ \int  rac{4x - 1}{(x - 1)(x + 3)}\,dx \] Click to reveal solutions P1.1 Set up: \[  rac{3x + 5}{(x + 1)(x + 2)} =  rac{A}{x + 1} +  rac{B}{x + 2}. \] Clear denominators: \[ 3x + 5 = A(x + 2) + B(x + 1). \] Expand: \[ 3x + 5 = (A + B)x + (2A + B). \] Match coefficients: \[ A + B = 3,\quad 2A + B = 5. \] Subtract: \[ A = 2,\quad B = 1. \] Integrate: \[ \int \left( rac{2}{x + 1} +  rac{1}{x + 2}ight)dx = 2\ln|x + 1| + \ln|x + 2| + C. \] P1.2 Set up: \[  rac{4x - 1}{(x - 1)(x + 3)} =  rac{A}{x - 1} +  rac{B}{x + 3}. \] Clear denominators: \[ 4x - 1 = A(x + 3) + B(x - 1). \] Expand: \[ 4x - 1 = (A + B)x + (3A - B). \] Match coefficients: \[ A + B = 4,\quad 3A - B = -1. \] Add: \[ 4A = 3 \Rightarrow A =  rac{3}{4}. \] Then: \[ B = 4 -  rac{3}{4} =  rac{13}{4}. \] Integrate: \[  rac{3}{4}\ln|x - 1| +  rac{13}{4}\ln|x + 3| + C. \] Type II: Repeated Linear Factors P2.1 \[ \int  rac{2x + 3}{(x - 1)^2}\,dx \] P2.2 \[ \int  rac{x + 1}{(x + 2)^2}\,dx \] Click to reveal solutions P2.1 Set up: \[  rac{2x + 3}{(x - 1)^2} =  rac{A}{x - 1} +  rac{B}{(x - 1)^2}. \] Clear denominators: \[ 2x + 3 = A(x - 1) + B. \] Choose \(x = 1\): \[ 2(1) + 3 = B \Rightarrow B = 5. \] Substitute back: \[ 2x + 3 = A(x - 1) + 5 \Rightarrow A = 2. \] Integrate: \[ \int \left( rac{2}{x - 1} +  rac{5}{(x - 1)^2}ight)dx = 2\ln|x - 1| -  rac{5}{x - 1} + C. \] P2.2 Set up: \[  rac{x + 1}{(x + 2)^2} =  rac{A}{x + 2} +  rac{B}{(x + 2)^2}. \] Clear denominators: \[ x + 1 = A(x + 2) + B. \] Choose \(x = -2\): \[ -1 = B. \] Substitute back: \[ x + 1 = A(x + 2) - 1 \Rightarrow A = 1. \] Integrate: \[ \int \left( rac{1}{x + 2} -  rac{1}{(x + 2)^2}ight)dx = \ln|x + 2| +  rac{1}{x + 2} + C. \] Type III: Quadratic Denominators That Don’t Factor These look like partial fractions problems, but the denominator doesn’t factor, so there’s nothing to decompose. Split the numerator or use substitution instead. P3.1 \[ \int  rac{2x + 1}{x^2 + 1}\,dx \] P3.2 \[ \int  rac{3x}{x^2 + 4}\,dx \] Click to reveal solutions P3.1 Split: \[ \int  rac{2x}{x^2 + 1}dx + \int  rac{1}{x^2 + 1}dx. \] First term (substitution): \[ u = x^2 + 1,\quad du = 2x\,dx \Rightarrow \ln(x^2 + 1). \] Second term: \[ \int  rac{1}{x^2 + 1}dx = \arctan x. \] Final: \[ \ln(x^2 + 1) + \arctan x + C. \] P3.2 Let: \[ u = x^2 + 4,\quad du = 2x\,dx. \] Rewrite: \[ \int  rac{3x}{x^2 + 4}dx =  rac{3}{2}\int  rac{1}{u}du. \] Integrate: \[  rac{3}{2}\ln(x^2 + 4) + C. \] Strategy Reminder Linear factors → logarithms Repeated factors → powers and logarithms Quadratics that don’t factor → substitution, and sometimes arctangent 5.8.5 Mixed Practice: Choosing and Executing the Right Method Real problems don’t tell you which technique they need. Diagnose first, then choose. Section 1: Which Method? For each integral below: Decide which method you would use (basic rules, substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions). Give a one-phrase justification. Do not compute yet. M1. \[ \int x^5 \, dx \] M2. \[ \int (3x^2 + 1)^4 \cdot 6x \, dx \] M3. \[ \int x e^x \, dx \] M4. \[ \int  rac{3x + 2}{(x - 1)(x + 2)} \, dx \] M5. \[ \int \cos(4x)\, dx \] M6. \[ \int \ln x \, dx \] M7. \[ \int  rac{2x}{x^2 + 5} \, dx \] M8. \[ \int x^2 e^x \, dx \] M9. \[ \int  rac{1}{(x - 3)^2} \, dx \] M10. \[ \int (x + 1)^7 \, dx \] Click to reveal method choices M1: Basic power rule M2: Substitution (nested function + derivative present) M3: Integration by parts (product; \(x\) simplifies when differentiated) M4: Partial fractions (rational function with factorable denominator) M5: Substitution (inner function off by a constant) M6: Integration by parts (implicit product \(\ln x \cdot 1\)) M7: Substitution (numerator is derivative of denominator up to constant) M8: Integration by parts (product; requires repetition) M9: Basic power rule (rewrite with negative exponent) M10: Basic power rule (simple polynomial) Section 2: Solve Now compute each integral using the method you identified above. Write your setup clearly before integrating. M1. \[ \int x^5 \, dx \] M2. \[ \int (3x^2 + 1)^4 \cdot 6x \, dx \] M3. \[ \int x e^x \, dx \] M4. \[ \int  rac{3x + 2}{(x - 1)(x + 2)} \, dx \] M5. \[ \int \cos(4x)\, dx \] M6. \[ \int \ln x \, dx \] M7. \[ \int  rac{2x}{x^2 + 5} \, dx \] M8. \[ \int x^2 e^x \, dx \] M9. \[ \int  rac{1}{(x - 3)^2} \, dx \] M10. \[ \int (x + 1)^7 \, dx \] Click to reveal solutions M1 \[  rac{x^6}{6} + C \] M2 Let \(u = 3x^2 + 1,\; du = 6x\,dx\) \[  rac{u^5}{5} + C =  rac{(3x^2 + 1)^5}{5} + C \] M3 \[ x e^x - e^x + C \] M4 Decompose: \[  rac{3x + 2}{(x - 1)(x + 2)} =  rac{5}{3(x - 1)} +  rac{4}{3(x + 2)} \] \[  rac{5}{3}\ln|x - 1| +  rac{4}{3}\ln|x + 2| + C \] M5 \[  rac{1}{4}\sin(4x) + C \] M6 \[ x \ln x - x + C \] M7 Let \(u = x^2 + 5,\; du = 2x\,dx\) \[ \ln(x^2 + 5) + C \] M8 Apply integration by parts twice: \[ x^2 e^x - 2x e^x + 2e^x + C \] M9 \[ - rac{1}{x - 3} + C \] M10 \[  rac{(x + 1)^8}{8} + C \] Final Reflection Did you identify the structure before computing? Did your method actually simplify the problem? Could you explain your choice in one sentence? Applications: Choosing and Applying a Technique in an Environmental Context For each problem, say which technique applies, then carry it out. The recognition step is the point. Applied 1: Soil Moisture Loss After Irrigation A 1 m² test plot has just been irrigated. The rate at which water leaves the topsoil (evaporation plus drainage) is modeled as \[  rac{dm}{dt} = -100\,e^{-0.05 t} \quad 	ext{(g/hr)}, \] where \(t\) is hours since irrigation ended. Find the total water lost between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 24\) hours. Click to reveal solution Technique: Substitution (with \(u = -0.05 t\), \(du = -0.05\,dt\)). Equivalently, the antiderivative of \(e^{kt}\) is \( rac{1}{k}e^{kt}\) from the dictionary. \[ \Delta m = \int_0^{24} -100\,e^{-0.05 t}\,dt = -100 \cdot  rac{1}{-0.05} igl[e^{-0.05 t} igr]_0^{24} = 2000 igl(e^{-1.2} - 1 igr). \] Numerically, \(e^{-1.2} \approx 0.3012\), so \[ \Delta m \approx 2000(0.3012 - 1) \approx -1398 	ext{ g}. \] The negative sign means water left the plot. About 1.4 kg of water (about 1.4 L, or 1.4 mm of depth over the plot) was lost in the first 24 hours. Applied 2: Pollutant Decay in a Small Pond A pulse of pollutant enters a small pond and degrades over time according to the rate \[  rac{dC}{dt} = - rac{50}{(0.1 t + 1)^2} \quad 	ext{(mg/L per day)}, \] where \(t\) is days since the pulse. Find the net change in concentration between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 9\) days. Click to reveal solution Technique: Substitution. Let \(u = 0.1 t + 1\), so \(du = 0.1\,dt\), or \(dt = 10\,du\). When \(t = 0\), \(u = 1\); when \(t = 9\), \(u = 1.9\). \[ \Delta C = \int_0^9 - rac{50}{(0.1 t + 1)^2}\,dt = -50 \cdot 10 \int_1^{1.9}  rac{du}{u^2} = -500\left[- rac{1}{u}ight]_1^{1.9} = -500\left(- rac{1}{1.9} + 1ight) \approx -500(0.4737) \approx -236.8 	ext{ mg/L}. \] The pond’s pollutant concentration decreased by about 236.8 mg/L over the nine-day window. Applied 3: Cumulative Microbial Respiration After a Substrate Pulse A pulse of glucose is added to a soil microcosm at \(t = 0\). The instantaneous CO₂ respiration rate of the microbial community is modeled as \[ R(t) = t\,e^{-t/2} \quad 	ext{(μg C per hour)}, \] where \(t\) is hours since the pulse. Find the total carbon respired between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 6\) hours. Click to reveal solution Technique: Integration by parts. The integrand is a product where one factor (\(t\)) simplifies under differentiation and the other (\(e^{-t/2}\)) is easy to integrate. Let \(u = t\), \(dv = e^{-t/2}\,dt\). Then \(du = dt\), \(v = -2 e^{-t/2}\). \[ \int t\,e^{-t/2}\,dt = -2 t e^{-t/2} - \int -2 e^{-t/2}\,dt = -2 t e^{-t/2} - 4 e^{-t/2} + C = -2 e^{-t/2}(t + 2) + C. \] Evaluate on \([0, 6]\): \[  igl[-2 e^{-t/2}(t + 2) igr]_0^6 = -2 e^{-3}(8) -  igl(-2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 igr) = -16 e^{-3} + 4. \] Numerically, \(e^{-3} \approx 0.0498\), so \[ 	ext{Total } \approx -16(0.0498) + 4 \approx 3.20 	ext{ μg C}. \] About 3.2 μg of carbon was respired by the community during the six-hour window after the glucose pulse. Applied 4: Heat Lost from a Cooling Storage Tank A large insulated storage tank cools after being filled with warm water. The rate at which heat is lost to the surroundings is modeled as \[ H(t) = (10 - t)\,e^{-t/2} \quad 	ext{(MJ/hr)}, \] where \(t\) is hours since filling. Find the total heat lost between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 10\) hours. Click to reveal solution Technique: Integration by parts. Let \(u = 10 - t\), \(dv = e^{-t/2}\,dt\). Then \(du = -dt\), \(v = -2 e^{-t/2}\). \[ \int (10 - t)\,e^{-t/2}\,dt = -2(10 - t) e^{-t/2} - \int -2 e^{-t/2} \cdot (-1)\,dt = -2(10 - t) e^{-t/2} - 2 e^{-t/2} + C. \] Simplify: \[ = -2 e^{-t/2} igl[(10 - t) + 1 igr] + C = -2 e^{-t/2}(11 - t) + C. \] Evaluate on \([0, 10]\): \[  igl[-2 e^{-t/2}(11 - t) igr]_0^{10} = -2 e^{-5}(1) - (-2 \cdot 1 \cdot 11) = -2 e^{-5} + 22. \] Numerically, \(e^{-5} \approx 0.00674\), so \[ 	ext{Total } \approx -0.013 + 22 \approx 21.99 	ext{ MJ}. \] About 22 MJ of heat is lost over the first ten hours. Applied 5: Two-Compartment Nutrient Transfer Nitrogen moves from soil into roots at a rate that falls off as the soil pool is drawn down: \[ r(t) =  rac{1}{(t+1)(t+3)} \quad 	ext{(g N/day)}, \] where \(t\) is days. Find the total transfer \[ T = \int_0^3  rac{1}{(t+1)(t+3)}\,dt. \] Evaluate \(T\) using partial fractions. Click to reveal solution Technique: Partial fractions. The denominator has two distinct linear factors and the derivative of the denominator isn’t sitting in the numerator. Decompose: \[  rac{1}{(t+1)(t+3)} =  rac{A}{t+1} +  rac{B}{t+3}. \] Clear the denominator: \(1 = A(t+3) + B(t+1)\). Plug in \(t = -1\): \(1 = 2A \Rightarrow A = 	frac{1}{2}\). Plug in \(t = -3\): \(1 = -2B \Rightarrow B = -	frac{1}{2}\). So \[ \int  rac{dt}{(t+1)(t+3)} = 	frac{1}{2}\ln|t+1| - 	frac{1}{2}\ln|t+3| + C = 	frac{1}{2}\ln\left| rac{t+1}{t+3}ight| + C. \] Evaluate on \([0, 3]\): \[ T = 	frac{1}{2}\left[\ln\left|	frac{4}{6}ight| - \ln\left|	frac{1}{3}ight|ight] = 	frac{1}{2}\left[\ln	frac{2}{3} - \ln	frac{1}{3}ight] = 	frac{1}{2}\ln 2 \approx 0.347. \] About 0.35 g of nitrogen moved into the roots over the three days. Applied 6: Choose and Apply, Leaf Photosynthesis During a brief flash of light, a leaf’s photosynthesis rate per unit area is modeled as \[ P(t) =  rac{6 t}{t^2 + 1} \quad 	ext{(μmol CO}_2	ext{/m}^2	ext{/s)}, \] where \(t\) is seconds since the flash began. Find the total CO₂ taken up per square meter of leaf between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 4\) seconds. Before computing, say which technique applies, and why the others don’t. Click to reveal solution Technique selection: Partial fractions? The integrand is a rational function with denominator \(t^2 + 1\), but the numerator is \(6t\), and the derivative of the denominator is \(2t\), which is sitting right there up to a factor of 3. That’s a substitution signal, not a partial-fractions signal. Integration by parts? No clean product where one factor simplifies on differentiation. Substitution with \(u = t^2 + 1\), \(du = 2t\,dt\), so \(6t\,dt = 3\,du\): \[ \int_0^4  rac{6t}{t^2 + 1}\,dt = 3 \int_1^{17}  rac{du}{u} = 3 igl[\ln u igr]_1^{17} = 3\ln 17. \] Numerically, \(\ln 17 \approx 2.833\), so \[ 	ext{Total uptake } \approx 3(2.833) \approx 8.50 	ext{ μmol CO}_2	ext{/m}^2. \] About 8.5 μmol of CO₂ per square meter of leaf was taken up during the four-second flash. The recognition lesson: a rational integrand where \(Q'(x)\) appears (up to a constant) in the numerator is a substitution problem, not a partial-fractions problem.
