Chapter 6 Applications of Integration Chapter 5 was about mechanics: rules and techniques. This chapter is about using them. Integrals answer a lot of different questions: how much rain fell, how much carbon a forest gained, the average flow during a spawning window, how much water ran above a minimum flow, the total biomass in a riparian strip. The math is the same each time. What changes is what you’re adding up, and what the answer means. 6.1 From Rates and Densities to Totals Most things you measure in the field aren’t totals. They’re amounts per unit of time or space: rainfall rate (mm per hour) population density (individuals per km²) carbon flux (kg of carbon per m² per year) streamflow (m³ per second) plankton concentration (cells per m³) leaf-area density in a canopy (m² of leaf per m³ of air) Each tells you what’s happening at one place or moment, not the total. 6.1.1 Small Pieces Add Up To get from a rate or density to a total, break the system into small pieces: Over a short time interval \(\Delta t\), a rain rate \(r(t)\) produces approximately \[ r(t)\,\Delta t \] units of rainfall. Over a small area \(\Delta A\), a density \(\rho(x,y)\) contains approximately \[ \rho(x,y)\,\Delta A \] units of mass or population. Each piece contributes a little, and the total is the sum of all of them. That’s the whole idea behind integration. 6.1.2 From Sums to Integrals Divide the interval into pieces and add up the contributions: \[ \text{total} \approx \sum (\text{rate or density}) \times (\text{size of piece}), \] That’s an approximation, the same idea as a Riemann sum. As the pieces get smaller, it gets better, and the limit is the integral: \[ \text{total} = \int (\text{rate or density}) \, (\text{unit of accumulation}). \] Integrate a rate over time and you get a total amount. Integrate a density over space and you get a total mass or count. Integrate a flux over area and time and you get a total transfer. 6.1.3 Units Tell the Story Units are one of the best ways to read an integral. Rainfall rate: mm/hour Multiply by time (hours) → mm of rainfall Population density: individuals/km² Multiply by area (km²) → number of individuals Carbon flux: kg/m²/year Multiply by area and time → kg of carbon Plankton concentration: cells/m³ Multiply by volume (m³) → number of cells Leaf-area density: m² of leaf area/m³ Multiply by volume (m³) → total leaf area The units of the integrand times the units of the differential give the units of the total. If those units make sense, the setup usually does too. 6.1.4 Accumulation, Not Just Area Integrals get introduced as “area under a curve,” but what matters is accumulation: how much built up over a period, how much is in a region, and how gains and losses combine. The rest of this chapter applies that one idea in different settings. Concept Check: Rates and Densities vs Totals What’s the difference between a rate, a density, and a total? And why can’t most environmental questions be answered by one alone? Click to reveal answer A rate is how fast something changes per unit time (rain falling at 5 mm/hr). A density is how much of something is packed into a unit of space (300 trees per hectare). A total is how much there is overall (47 mm of rain this storm, 12,000 trees in the watershed). Most environmental questions are about totals, but what you can measure is usually a rate or a density. The integral gets you from one to the other. Concept Check: Why Multiplication Isn’t Enough If a rainfall sensor reports 5 mm/hr, why can’t you just multiply by the duration of the storm to get the total rainfall? Click to reveal answer Because real rates don’t stay constant. The 5 mm/hr reading is a snapshot. Ten minutes later the storm will be heavier or lighter. Multiplying one reading by the whole duration pretends the rate never changed. Integration adds up many short pieces, each with the rate that applied during it. 6.2 Accumulation When Totals Are Always Positive Sometimes accumulation only goes one way. Every contribution adds to the total and nothing is taken away, so the total is never negative. These are the easiest integrals to interpret. 6.2.1 Examples of Always-Positive Accumulation Total rainfall over time The rain rate varies, but rain only adds water. Integrate the rate over time and you get total precipitation. Total distance traveled If speed is never negative, integrating speed over time gives distance, which only goes up. Total water collected Integrate an inflow rate into a reservoir and you get the volume added (as long as the model ignores outflow). Total biomass produced Integrate a production rate (plant growth, primary productivity) and you get the biomass produced over a season. Plankton in a water column Integrate plankton concentration over depth and you get the total count per unit of surface area. In each case, the integrand can’t be negative, and the integral tells you how much, not a balance between competing processes. That makes these good examples to build intuition on before signed cases. Concept Check: What Makes an Accumulation “Always Positive” Why is total rainfall over a storm an “always-positive” accumulation, but net carbon exchange for a forest over a day is not? Click to reveal answer Rainfall only adds: drops can’t un-fall. So the rate is never negative, and neither is its integral. Net carbon exchange has a signed rate. Photosynthesis pulls carbon in (positive) and respiration releases it (negative), and both are happening at once. Depending on the time of day and season, either can win, so the integral can come out positive, negative or zero. Concept Check: Reading Units to Find the Total A leaf-level photosynthesis rate is reported as μmol CO₂ / m² / s. You integrate it over time and over the leaf area. What units does the result have? Click to reveal answer Multiplying by seconds cancels the “/s”, leaving μmol CO₂/m². Multiplying by m² cancels the “/m²”, leaving μmol CO₂. Tracking units like this is one of the fastest ways to catch a setup error. If the final units don’t match the quantity you’re after, the integral is wrong. 6.3 Net Accumulation: When Gains and Losses Compete Most environmental systems gain and lose at the same time: growth and decay, inflow and outflow, uptake and release. Here the integral gives the net accumulation. The math is the same. The interpretation changes. 6.3.1 Signed Contributions Matter When a rate can be positive or negative, each small piece has a sign. Positive pieces add to the total and negative pieces subtract. Over a short interval \(\Delta t\), a rate \(r(t)\) contributes approximately \[ r(t)\,\Delta t, \] which may increase or decrease the accumulated amount depending on the sign of \(r(t)\). The integral adds them all, signs included: \[ \text{net change} = \int r(t)\,dt. \] So instead of “how much was added?”, the question is now “what’s the balance once gains and losses are combined?" 6.3.2 Common Examples of Net Accumulation A river reach Water comes in from upstream and is lost to evaporation and groundwater. Integrate the net flow and you get the change in stored water. An ecosystem’s carbon balance Photosynthesis adds carbon and respiration releases it. Integrate net carbon flux and you get the net gain or loss. A contaminant in a lake Inflow brings it in. Outflow and breakdown remove it. Integrate the net rate and you get the change in the lake’s contaminant load. A population Births add individuals and deaths remove them. Integrate births minus deaths and you get the net change. Heat Heat can enter and leave a system at the same time. The integral gives the net energy gained. The total isn’t guaranteed to go up. It depends on which process wins. 6.3.3 Signed Area Geometrically, net accumulation is signed area: area above the axis counts as positive, area below as negative. Two regions of the same size and opposite sign cancel. A net of zero doesn’t mean nothing happened. It means gains and losses balanced. This is how integrals handle balance laws, the bookkeeping at the heart of most environmental models: what comes in, what goes out, and what’s left. Keep the two kinds apart: Always-positive accumulation tells you how much. Net accumulation tells you what’s left after everything is accounted for. Concept Check: When Net Differs from Total Suppose a stream gains 800 m³ of water during a storm and loses 800 m³ in the days following through evaporation and seepage. The net accumulation over the period is zero. What is the total accumulation? And which one would you report if asked “how much water moved through this system?” Click to reveal answer Net accumulation is zero, because the gains and losses cancel in the signed integral. Total accumulation (integrating |rate| instead of the rate) is 1,600 m³, the volume of water that actually moved. Which to report depends on the question. “Did the system gain or lose water?” is net. “How much water moved through it?” is total. Concept Check: Negative Integrands and Signed Areas If the rate of net population change for a fish stock is negative for several months out of a year, what does the integral of that rate over those months contribute to the year-end net change? Click to reveal answer A negative number: a population loss. Where the integrand is below the axis, it contributes negative “area.” That’s why the year’s net change can be zero or even negative: the good months and the bad months compete in the same sum. 6.4 Using Integrals to Compute the Average Value of a Function An average is a typical value: the average temperature over a day, rainfall over a season, pollution over a region. When the quantity changes continuously, the integral gives you a precise way to compute it. 6.4.1 Average as “Total Divided by Size” For a list of values, \[ \text{average} = \frac{\text{sum of values}}{\text{number of values}}. \] For a function, the integral gives the total, and you divide by the length of the interval to spread it out evenly. 6.4.2 Definition: Average Value of a Function If \(f(x)\) is continuous on the interval \([a,b]\), its average value on that interval is \[ f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx. \] The integral is the total. Dividing by \(b-a\) turns it into an average per unit of \(x\). 6.4.3 Picturing It Replace the curve with a flat line at height \(f_{\text{avg}}\). The rectangle of height \(f_{\text{avg}}\) and width \(b-a\) has the same area as the region under the curve: \[ (b-a)\,f_{\text{avg}} = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx. \] So the average value is the height of the rectangle with the same total. Example: Average Value of \(x^2\) on \([2,4]\) Let \[ f(x) = x^2. \] We want to find the average value of \(f(x)\) on the interval \([2,4]\). Step 1: Write the Average Value Formula The average value of a function on \([a,b]\) is \[ f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx. \] Here, \(a = 2\) and \(b = 4\), so \[ f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{4-2}\int_2^4 x^2\,dx. \] Step 2: Compute the Integral An antiderivative of \(x^2\) is \[ \int x^2\,dx = \frac{x^3}{3}. \] Evaluate from 2 to 4: \[ \int_2^4 x^2\,dx = \left.\frac{x^3}{3}\right|_2^4 = \frac{4^3}{3} - \frac{2^3}{3} = \frac{64 - 8}{3} = \frac{56}{3}. \] Step 3: Divide by the Interval Length The interval length is \(4 - 2 = 2\), so \[ f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{56}{3} = \frac{28}{3}. \] Final Answer The average value of \(x^2\) on the interval \([2,4]\) is \[ \boxed{\frac{28}{3}}. \] Interpretation A flat line at \(y = \tfrac{28}{3}\) has the same total area over \([2,4]\) as \(y = x^2\). A rectangle of height \(\tfrac{28}{3}\) and width 2 holds the same total as the curve. 6.4.4 Environmental Examples Average temperature over a day: integrate temperature over time and divide by 24 hours. Average rainfall rate during a storm: total rainfall divided by the storm’s duration. Average plankton concentration with depth: integrate over depth and divide by the total depth. Average pollutant concentration along a reach: integrate over distance and divide by the reach length. 6.4.5 Signed Functions and Averages If \(f(x)\) is positive in some places and negative in others, the average reflects the net. Positive regions pull it up, negative regions pull it down, and big regions of each can cancel. An average of zero doesn’t mean nothing happened. Concept Check: Why Average = (1/(b-a)) ∫ f dx Makes Sense The average value of \(f\) on \([a, b]\) is \(\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). Why does that formula make sense intuitively? Click to reveal answer The integral is the total of \(f\) over the interval. Dividing by the width \(b - a\) gives the constant value that would produce the same total over the same interval: the height of a flat line with the same area. That’s what an average is: the steady value that adds up to the same thing as the real, varying one. Concept Check: Average Rate in Environmental Context A daily streamflow record for a river over a year gives a function \(Q(t)\). What does \(\frac{1}{365}\int_0^{365} Q(t)\,dt\) tell you, and why is it more useful than knowing \(Q\) at any single day? Click to reveal answer It’s the average discharge over the year: the steady flow that, running for 365 days, would move the same total volume of water as the real flow did. It’s more useful than any one day’s reading because it smooths over storms, droughts and day-to-day noise and gives you one number to compare across years or rivers. 6.5 Area Between Two Curves Sometimes what you want isn’t accumulation relative to the axis, but the gap between two functions over the same interval: an observed curve and a target, upper and lower bounds, two competing models. Integration gives you that area between curves. 6.5.1 The Core Idea Suppose we have two functions: \(f(x)\): the upper curve \(g(x)\): the lower curve on an interval \([a,b]\). At each value of \(x\), the vertical distance between the curves is \[ f(x) - g(x). \] If we break the interval into small pieces of width \(\Delta x\), each thin vertical strip has approximate area \[ \big(f(x) - g(x)\big)\Delta x. \] Adding up all of these strips leads to the integral: \[ \text{Area} = \int_a^b \big[f(x) - g(x)\big]\,dx. \] 6.5.2 Why This Always Produces a Positive Area Area is geometric, not signed. Subtracting the lower curve from the upper one makes the height of every strip positive. That’s different from net accumulation, where positive and negative contributions cancel. Area between curves measures separation, not balance. 6.5.3 Environmental and Scientific Examples Temperature range The area between daily maximum and minimum temperature curves adds up the day-to-day temperature range over a season. Uncertainty bands The area between the upper and lower prediction curves measures total uncertainty across the range of a model. Water table and bedrock Along a transect, the area between the water table and the bedrock surface is the saturated cross-section of the aquifer, per meter of width. Multiply by porosity to get the water stored. Example: Extra Water Stored Above a “Minimum Flow” Target A river manager wants to keep a minimum ecological flow of 30 m³/s for fish habitat. During spring snowmelt the river runs above that target. The extra water above the target is what could be stored, released later or left to recharge the floodplain. Let \(t\) be time in days over a 10-day period, and let streamflow be measured in m³/s. Define: Actual flow (a simple “spring pulse” model): \[ Q(t) = 30 + 10\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{10}\right) \quad \text{m}^3/\text{s} \] Target minimum flow: \[ Q_{\min}(t) = 30 \quad \text{m}^3/\text{s} \] What does the area between curves represent? The difference \[ Q(t) - Q_{\min}(t) = 10\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{10}\right) \] is the extra discharge above the minimum flow (m³/s). If we integrate this over time, we get extra volume of water: \[ \int_0^{10} \big(Q(t) - Q_{\min}(t)\big)\,dt \quad \Rightarrow \quad (\text{m}^3/\text{s})\cdot(\text{time}) \] To make units intuitive, convert days to seconds: \[ 1\ \text{day} = 86400\ \text{s}. \] So the extra volume (in m³) is: \[ V_{\text{extra}} = 86400\int_0^{10} 10\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{10}\right)\,dt. \] Compute the integral \[ \int 10\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{10}\right)\,dt = 10\left(-\frac{10}{\pi}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{10}\right) = -\frac{100}{\pi}\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{10}\right). \] Evaluate from 0 to 10: \[ \int_0^{10} 10\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{10}\right)\,dt = \left[-\frac{100}{\pi}\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{10}\right)\right]_0^{10} \] \[ = -\frac{100}{\pi}\cos(\pi) - \left(-\frac{100}{\pi}\cos(0)\right) = -\frac{100}{\pi}(-1) + \frac{100}{\pi}(1) = \frac{200}{\pi}. \] Now convert to volume: \[ V_{\text{extra}} = 86400\cdot \frac{200}{\pi} = \frac{17,\!280,\!000}{\pi} \approx 5,\!501,\!000\ \text{m}^3. \] Result and Interpretation \[ \boxed{V_{\text{extra}} \approx 5.50\times 10^6\ \text{m}^3} \] That’s the extra volume of water delivered above the ecological minimum over the 10-day pulse. Example: Population Change from Birth and Death Rates Populations change because individuals are born and die all the time. Instead of counting individuals, we model the two processes as rates and integrate the difference to get the net change in population. Model setup Let \(t\) represent time in years, with \(0 \le t \le 10\). Define: - Birth rate: \[ B(t) = 120 + 20\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right) \quad \text{individuals/year} \] - Death rate: \[ D(t) = 100 + 10\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right) \quad \text{individuals/year} \] Births swing more (seasonal reproduction). Deaths swing less, around a lower baseline. What the gap between the curves means At any time \(t\), the difference \[ B(t) - D(t) \] is the net rate of population change (individuals per year). Where \(B(t) > D(t)\) the population is growing, and where \(B(t) < D(t)\) it’s shrinking. The integral \[ \int_0^{10} \big[B(t) - D(t)\big]\,dt \] is the signed area between the curves: the net change in population over 10 years. (The curves cross briefly, so this is a net, not a geometric area.) Compute the net population change First compute the difference: \[ B(t) - D(t) = (120 - 100) + 20\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right) - 10\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right). \] Integrate term by term: \[ \int_0^{10} 20\,dt = 200, \] \[ \int_0^{10} 20\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right)\,dt = 20\left[-\frac{5}{\pi}\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right)\right]_0^{10} = 0, \] \[ \int_0^{10} 10\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right)\,dt = 10\left[\frac{5}{\pi}\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right)\right]_0^{10} = 0. \] So the oscillating terms cancel over the full interval, leaving: \[ \int_0^{10} \big[B(t) - D(t)\big]\,dt = 200. \] Result and interpretation \[ \boxed{\text{Net population change over 10 years} = 200\ \text{individuals}} \] The population gains 200 individuals overall. Births and deaths both swing around a lot, but over the full 10 years the swings cancel, and what’s left is the difference between the baselines: 20 per year for 10 years. Big picture Carbon uptake against release, inflow against outflow, growth against decay: the same setup works for all of them. The integral of the difference turns two competing processes into one number you can interpret. 6.5.4 When the Curves Cross If the curves cross, “upper” and “lower” swap. To get the geometric area: Find where they intersect. Split the interval so one function stays on top in each piece. Compute top minus bottom on each piece and add them up. Sketch the curves first. It’s the easiest way to get the setup right. Concept Check: Top Minus Bottom For \(\int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)]\,dx\) to represent a positive area between two curves, what has to be true about \(f\) and \(g\) on \([a, b]\)? And what happens if the curves cross within the interval? Click to reveal answer You need \(f(x) \geq g(x)\) across all of \([a, b]\): \(f\) is the top curve and \(g\) the bottom. If the curves cross, the labels swap at the crossing and the integrand changes sign. To get the geometric area, split at every crossing and integrate \(|f - g|\) piece by piece. Otherwise the regions where \(g\) is on top cancel some of the area where \(f\) is on top. Concept Check: What ‘Area Between’ Means Environmentally If \(Q_{\text{actual}}(t)\) is the actual streamflow on day \(t\) and \(Q_{\text{min}}\) is a constant minimum ecological flow, what physical quantity does \(\int_0^{365} [Q_{\text{actual}}(t) - Q_{\text{min}}]\,dt\) compute when the actual flow exceeds the minimum throughout? Click to reveal answer The total volume of “extra” water: water that flowed above the ecological threshold over the year. Each day contributes the excess flow times one day, and the integral adds them up. If the flow ever dropped below the minimum, those days would count negatively. To get only the surplus, you’d integrate just over the periods when the flow was above the minimum. 6.6 Double Integrals: Accumulation Over Two Dimensions So far we’ve accumulated over one variable: time, distance or depth. A lot of environmental quantities vary over two spatial dimensions at once, like biomass across a riparian zone or rainfall across a watershed. To add up over a whole region, you need a double integral. 6.6.1 From Length to Area The idea hasn’t changed. A function value is an “amount per unit,” a small piece times that value is a contribution, and the total is all the contributions added up. The only difference is the shape of the piece. Instead of thin intervals of width \(dx\), break the region into small patches of area \[ \Delta A \approx \Delta x\,\Delta y. \] Each small rectangle contributes approximately \[ f(x,y)\,\Delta A. \] Adding up all such contributions leads to a double integral. 6.6.2 Definition: Double Integral Over a Region If \(f(x,y)\) represents a density, rate, or intensity over a region \(R\), then the total amount is \[ \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA. \] \(f(x,y)\) is the amount per unit area at \((x,y)\), \(dA\) is a tiny patch of area, and the double integral adds up contributions from everywhere in the region. 6.6.3 Units Still Tell the Story Units help even more here. Examples: Population density (individuals/km²) \(\times\) area (km²) → total population Rainfall rate (mm/hour) over a landscape \(\times\) area \(\times\) time → total rainfall volume Pollutant mass per unit area (kg/m²) \(\times\) area → total pollutant mass Heat flux per unit area (W/m²) \(\times\) area → total heat transfer rate If the units multiply out to a sensible total, the integral is set up right. 6.6.4 Rectangular Regions and Iterated Integrals When the region \(R\) is rectangular, \[ R = \{(x,y)\mid a \le x \le b,\; c \le y \le d\}, \] the double integral can be computed as an iterated integral: \[ \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx = \int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx\,dy. \] Integrate in one variable while treating the other as a constant, then integrate the result in the other variable. For a well-behaved \(f\), either order gives the same total. 6.6.5 Interpretation: Stacking Integrals Think of it as a stack of single integrals. Fix \(x\) and integrate \(f(x,y)\) over \(y\): that’s the total along one strip. Then integrate the strip totals over \(x\) to add up all the strips. It’s a Riemann sum in two directions instead of one. Double integrals take you from measurements at points to totals over landscapes and regions. The math extends what you already know. The shift is that you’re adding up across an area instead of along a line. Example: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Rectangle Just the mechanics, step by step. Let \[ f(x,y) = x^2 + xy - y, \] and consider the rectangular region \[ R = \{(x,y)\mid -5 \le x \le 5,\; -2 \le y \le 2\}. \] We want to evaluate \[ \iint_R \big(x^2 + xy - y\big)\,dA. \] Step 1: Write as an iterated integral Because \(R\) is rectangular, we can integrate with respect to either variable first. We’ll integrate with respect to \(y\) first: \[ \iint_R \big(x^2 + xy - y\big)\,dA = \int_{-5}^{5} \int_{-2}^{2} \big(x^2 + xy - y\big)\,dy\,dx. \] Step 2: Integrate with respect to \(y\) Treat \(x\) as a constant: \[ \int_{-2}^{2} (x^2 + xy - y)\,dy = \left[x^2y + \frac{x}{2}y^2 - \frac{1}{2}y^2\right]_{-2}^{2}. \] Evaluate term by term: \(x^2y\): \(x^2(2 - (-2)) = 4x^2\) \(\frac{x}{2}y^2\): same at \(y=2\) and \(y=-2\), so it cancels \(-\frac{1}{2}y^2\): same at \(y=2\) and \(y=-2\), so it cancels So the result of the inner integral is: \[ 4x^2. \] Step 3: Integrate with respect to \(x\) Now integrate with respect to \(x\): \[ \int_{-5}^{5} 4x^2\,dx = 4\int_{-5}^{5} x^2\,dx = 4\left[ \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_{-5}^{5}. \] Evaluate: \[ = 4\left(\frac{125}{3} - \left(-\frac{125}{3}\right)\right) = 4\cdot\frac{250}{3} = \frac{1000}{3}. \] Final Answer \[ \boxed{\iint_R \big(x^2 + xy - y\big)\,dA = \frac{1000}{3}}. \] Notice With symmetric bounds, odd terms cancel on their own: \(xy\) and \(-y\) are odd in \(y\), so they integrate to zero over \([-2, 2]\). Each step is ordinary single-variable integration, one variable at a time. Graphically ## [1] 336.6792 Example: Integrating \(f(x,y)=x^2+xy-y\) Without Bounds What happens if we don’t apply bounds? Without bounds you’re not computing a total over a region. You’re finding an antiderivative. In more than one variable, the “constant of integration” becomes an arbitrary function of the other variable, because that variable was being treated as a constant. Let \[ f(x,y)=x^2+xy-y. \] Integrate with respect to \(y\) (treat \(x\) as constant) \[ \int \big(x^2+xy-y\big)\,dy \] Integrate term-by-term: \[ \int x^2\,dy = x^2y, \qquad \int xy\,dy = x\cdot\frac{y^2}{2}, \qquad \int (-y)\,dy = -\frac{y^2}{2}. \] So, \[ \int \big(x^2+xy-y\big)\,dy = x^2y+\frac{x}{2}y^2-\frac{y^2}{2}+C(x). \] Here \(C(x)\) is an arbitrary function of \(x\), because differentiating with respect to \(y\) makes any \(C(x)\) disappear. Integrate with respect to \(x\) (treat \(y\) as constant) \[ \int \big(x^2+xy-y\big)\,dx \] Again term-by-term: \[ \int x^2\,dx = \frac{x^3}{3}, \qquad \int xy\,dx = y\cdot\frac{x^2}{2}, \qquad \int (-y)\,dx = -yx. \] So, \[ \int \big(x^2+xy-y\big)\,dx = \frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{y}{2}x^2-yx+K(y). \] Here \(K(y)\) is an arbitrary function of \(y\), because differentiating with respect to \(x\) makes any \(K(y)\) disappear. So Without bounds you get a family of functions, not a number: \(\int f(x,y)\,dy\) gives \(F(x,y)+C(x)\), and \(\int f(x,y)\,dx\) gives \(G(x,y)+K(y)\). To get a number, you need bounds: a region. Concept Check: What ∫∫f(x,y) dA Represents for a Density Suppose \(\rho(x, y)\) gives the biomass density (kg per m²) at position \((x, y)\) in a riparian zone \(R\). What does \(\iint_R \rho(x, y)\,dA\) compute, and what are its units? Click to reveal answer The total biomass in the riparian zone. The integrand is in kg/m² and \(dA\) is in m², so the result is in kg. You’re cutting the zone into tiny patches, multiplying each patch’s area by the biomass density there, and adding them all up. Concept Check: Why Iterated Integrals Work Why can a double integral over a rectangular region be computed as two single integrals, one inside the other, rather than requiring some new “2D” integration technique? Click to reveal answer Because you can slice the region into thin strips. Integrate along each strip first (an ordinary integral in one variable), then add up the strip totals along the other direction (another ordinary integral). Each step is a regular definite integral. Fubini’s theorem is the formal result that says this works, and that the order doesn’t matter for well-behaved functions on a rectangle. 6.7 Triple Integrals: Accumulation Over Volume Double integrals go from a line to an area. Triple integrals go one step further, to a volume. If a quantity varies in all three directions (across, along and with depth), model it as \[ f(x,y,z), \] and integrate over a volume \(V\). The total amount is written as \[ \iiint_V f(x,y,z)\,dV. \] \(f(x,y,z)\) is an amount per unit volume, \(dV\) is a tiny volume element, and the triple integral adds up every small volume inside \(V\). 6.7.1 Iterated Form If the region is rectangular, \[ V = \{(x,y,z)\mid a \le x \le b,\; c \le y \le d,\; e \le z \le f\}, \] the triple integral can be computed as an iterated integral: \[ \iiint_V f(x,y,z)\,dV = \int_a^b \int_c^d \int_e^f f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx. \] As before, you integrate one variable at a time, treating the others as constants. Concept Check: When You’d Need a Triple Integral in Environmental Science Give an example of a quantity that would naturally be computed with a triple integral over a volume, and explain why three dimensions are needed. Click to reveal answer Total dissolved oxygen in a lake. Oxygen concentration \(c(x, y, z)\) varies across the lake (temperature, sunlight, wind mixing) and with depth (stratification, where the algae are, oxygen demand from the sediments). Integrating \(c\) over the lake’s volume gives total dissolved oxygen. A double integral over the surface would miss the depth structure, and in a stratified lake that’s most of the story. Concept Check: Units When Integrating Over Volume If \(\rho(x, y, z)\) has units of g of pollutant per m³, what are the units of \(\iiint_V \rho\,dV\) and what does the result represent? Click to reveal answer The volume element \(dV\) has units of m³, which cancels the “per m³” in the density, leaving units of grams. The integral represents the total mass of pollutant within the volume \(V\). 6.8 Quadruple Integrals: When Time Enters the Picture A quadruple integral comes up when a quantity varies in three dimensions of space and in time. For example, suppose \[ f(x,y,z,t) \] represents a density or rate that varies in space and time. To compute the total accumulated amount over a time interval and a spatial volume, we integrate over all four variables: \[ \iiiint f(x,y,z,t)\,dV\,dt. \] The triple integral over \(x,y,z\) gives a total at one moment. The outer integral over \(t\) adds those up over time. 6.8.1 Iterated Form For a rectangular space–time region, \[ a \le x \le b,\quad c \le y \le d,\quad e \le z \le f,\quad t_0 \le t \le t_1, \] the integral becomes \[ \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \int_a^b \int_c^d \int_e^f f(x,y,z,t)\,dz\,dy\,dx\,dt. \] Concept Check: Why Adding Time Turns 3D Into 4D If you already know how to compute the total pollutant mass in a lake at one moment using a triple integral over volume, why might a quadruple integral over volume and time be necessary? Click to reveal answer Because the distribution changes over time. A triple integral at one moment gives you the mass then. If you want something like the total exposure (mass × hours) over a week, you have to follow how the distribution changes and add it up over time as well. That’s the fourth integral. Concept Check: When You’d Actually Use a Quadruple Integral Give a concrete environmental setting where a quadruple integral (over space + time) is the right tool, and one where it’s overkill. Click to reveal answer Right tool: the total UV dose delivered to a lake’s surface waters over a summer. Intensity varies with position, depth and time, and what matters biologically is the cumulative dose. Overkill: the volume of a lake. Its shape doesn’t change over a short window, so a triple integral over space is enough. Adding time would just multiply the answer by the length of the window. 6.9 Big Picture Each step up in dimension follows the same logic: Single integral: along a line Double integral: over an area Triple integral: through a volume Quadruple integral: through a volume and over time The mechanics stay the same. What grows is the size of the thing you’re adding up over. 6.10 Numerical Integration: When No Nice Formula Exists So far we’ve assumed you have a formula to integrate. Real data don’t arrive that way. You get measurements: readings at set times, samples at set places, sometimes at uneven intervals. One option is to fit a curve to the data and integrate the curve. If the fit is smooth and sensible, that works well. But sometimes the data are noisy, the process is messy, nothing simple fits, or the fitted function is too complicated to integrate by hand. Forcing a “nice” curve then adds more error than it removes. That’s when you use numerical integration. 6.10.1 The Core Idea Numerical integration goes back to the original idea: add up many small contributions. Break the interval into pieces, approximate the function on each piece using your data, and add the pieces. It’s a Riemann sum built from real measurements. 6.10.2 Common Numerical Methods Left and right Riemann sums: use the value at one end of each subinterval. Midpoint rule: uses the value at the center, which is usually more accurate. Trapezoidal rule: uses trapezoids instead of rectangles. Simpson’s rule: fits parabolas across pairs of subintervals, for even more accuracy on smooth data. Each trades simplicity against accuracy differently. All of them estimate an integral from a finite set of values. Concept Check: When Numerical Integration Is Needed Give two situations in environmental science where you’d reach for numerical integration instead of trying to find an analytic antiderivative. Click to reveal answer You only have data, not a formula. A flux tower gives you half-hourly carbon-exchange readings. There’s no formula to antidifferentiate, so you integrate the data directly. The integrand has no elementary antiderivative. Functions like \(e^{-x^2}\) (the Gaussian, common in dispersion models) and \(\sin(x)/x\) show up in environmental work but have no antiderivative you can write down. Numerical methods give you the definite integral anyway. Concept Check: Choosing Among Numerical Methods What’s the trade-off between using a left-endpoint Riemann sum, the trapezoidal rule, and Simpson’s rule on the same dataset? Click to reveal answer Left-endpoint Riemann sum: simple and fast, but it’s always too high or too low when the rate only rises or only falls. Halving the step size only halves the error. Trapezoidal rule: a straight line across each step. Halving the step size cuts the error by about four. Usually a big improvement for smooth rates. Simpson’s rule: a parabola across each pair of steps. Halving the step size cuts the error by about sixteen. Often the best choice for smooth rates with evenly spaced data. The trade-off: the fancier methods get more accuracy out of each data point, but they assume the function is smoother. 6.11 Comparing Analytic and Numerical Integration from Data In the example below, the total streamflow over a year is computed two ways: Integrate a fitted function. Fit a smooth sinusoidal model to the daily data, then integrate the model. Integrate the data directly. Treat each daily measurement as a rectangle one day wide and add up the rectangles. The results (flow in m³/s times seconds, so the totals are in m³): Total from integrating the fitted curve: 1,252,203,685 m³ Total from adding up daily rectangles: 1,255,666,364 m³ Difference: 3,462,679 m³ 6.11.1 What These Numbers Mean The two totals agree to within about 0.3%. The difference comes from a few places: The fitted curve smooths over day-to-day variation. The rectangles use each day’s value as a flat step. Random noise in the data affects the rectangles directly, but mostly averages out in the fit. The difference isn’t a mistake. It comes from the modeling choice. If you can justify a smooth model, integrating it gives a clean answer. If you can’t, numerical integration gives you a total straight from the observations. Doing both and comparing them tells you how sensitive your answer is to that choice. In applied work, numerical integration is often the default, not the exception. Even when there’s no formula, you can still get a meaningful total. Concept Check: Model vs Data: When They Disagree If you fit a smooth model to streamflow data and integrate the model, you get one answer for total annual volume. If you instead apply Simpson’s rule directly to the raw daily measurements, you get a slightly different answer. Which one should you trust? Click to reveal answer Neither is automatically right. The fitted-model integral reflects the shape you assumed (a sinusoid, say). It’s smooth and easy to report, but it can miss real spikes. Integrating the data directly captures whatever the sensor recorded, noise included. If the two differ by more than your measurement uncertainty, your model is missing something real. Ask which features of the data the model is smoothing away. Concept Check: When to Trust Analytic, When to Trust Numerical What’s the practical guideline for choosing analytic vs numerical integration for a real environmental dataset? Click to reveal answer Integrate a formula when you have a model for the rate you can defend (fitted to data, based on the physics, or both) and the function has an antiderivative you can find. The answer is exact and reproducible. Integrate numerically when you only have data, or when the model has no antiderivative you can write down. Report the method and step size along with the answer, because the result depends on both. Often the strongest approach is to report both, and explain any difference. 6.12 Practice Problems These cover every application in the chapter: totals from rates and densities, net accumulation, average value, area between curves, double integrals and numerical methods. Some tell you which technique to use. Others ask you to decide. Problem 1: Total Rainfall from a Storm Hyetograph A storm gauge records rainfall intensity over a 4-hour storm as \[ r(t) = 3t - \tfrac{1}{2}t^2 \quad \text{(mm/hr)}, \] where \(t\) is hours since the storm started. Find the total rainfall over the 4-hour storm. Click to reveal solution This is an always-positive accumulation (\(r(t) \geq 0\) on \([0, 4]\)). \[ \int_0^4 \left(3t - \tfrac{1}{2}t^2\right) dt = \left[\tfrac{3}{2}t^2 - \tfrac{1}{6}t^3\right]_0^4 = 24 - \tfrac{64}{6} = 24 - 10.\overline{6} \approx 13.33 \text{ mm}. \] Total rainfall ≈ 13.3 mm. Problem 2: Net Carbon Exchange Over 24 Hours A flux tower in a young forest stand records net carbon flux as \[ F(t) = 0.4\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi (t - 6)}{12}\right) - 0.1 \quad \text{(g C / m}^2\text{/hr)}, \] where \(t\) is hours after midnight. Uptake peaks at noon. Find the net carbon exchange over a full 24-hour day, and interpret the sign. Click to reveal solution \[ \int_0^{24} \left[0.4\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi (t-6)}{12}\right) - 0.1\right] dt = \left[-\tfrac{4.8}{\pi}\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi (t-6)}{12}\right) - 0.1\,t\right]_0^{24}. \] At \(t = 24\): \(-\tfrac{4.8}{\pi}\cos\!\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) - 2.4 = 0 - 2.4 = -2.4\). At \(t = 0\): \(-\tfrac{4.8}{\pi}\cos\!\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - 0 = 0\). Difference: \[ -2.4 - 0 = -2.4 \text{ g C / m}^2. \] Net flux = −2.4 g C/m² over the day. The stand is a net carbon source that day. The sine part averages to zero over 24 hours, so what’s left is the constant 0.1 g/m²/hr of extra respiration, times 24 hours. Problem 3: Average Streamflow During a Spawning Window Over a 60-day spawning window, the daily mean streamflow in a river is modeled as \[ Q(t) = 80 + 20\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{30}\right) \quad \text{(m}^3\text{/s)}, \] where \(t\) is days into the window. Find the average streamflow over the window. Click to reveal solution \[ \bar{Q} = \frac{1}{60}\int_0^{60}\left[80 + 20\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi t}{30}\right)\right] dt = \frac{1}{60}\left[80 t - \tfrac{600}{\pi}\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi t}{30}\right)\right]_0^{60}. \] At \(t = 60\): \(4800 - \tfrac{600}{\pi}\cos(2\pi) = 4800 - \tfrac{600}{\pi}\). At \(t = 0\): \(0 - \tfrac{600}{\pi}\cos(0) = -\tfrac{600}{\pi}\). Difference: \(4800 - \tfrac{600}{\pi} + \tfrac{600}{\pi} = 4800\). \[ \bar{Q} = \frac{4800}{60} = 80 \text{ m}^3\text{/s}. \] Average streamflow = 80 m³/s. (The sinusoidal variation averages to zero over a full period, leaving just the baseline.) Problem 4: Water Above an Ecological-Flow Minimum A river has a regulatory minimum ecological flow of \(Q_{\text{min}} = 30\) m³/s. Over a 10-day window, the actual flow is \[ Q(t) = 30 + 12 t - t^2 \quad \text{(m}^3\text{/s)}, \] where \(t\) is days. Compute the total volume of water that flowed above the minimum during the window. (Careful with units: m³/s × days.) Click to reveal solution The excess flow is \(Q(t) - Q_{\text{min}} = 12t - t^2\). Check that this is positive on \([0, 10]\): \(12t - t^2 = t(12 - t) \geq 0\) for \(0 \leq t \leq 12\). \[ \int_0^{10} (12 t - t^2)\, dt = \left[6 t^2 - \tfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^{10} = 600 - \tfrac{1000}{3} \approx 266.67 \text{ (m}^3\text{/s)} \cdot \text{days}. \] Convert to m³: 1 day = 86,400 s, so \[ 266.67 \times 86{,}400 \approx 2.30 \times 10^7 \text{ m}^3. \] Total volume above the minimum ≈ 23 million m³ over the 10-day window. Problem 5: Net Population Change (Births vs Deaths) In a 6-month survey of juvenile salmon in a stream reach, fish arrive from upstream at a rate \(B(t) = 200 - 10t\) (fish/month) and die at a rate \(D(t) = 50 + 5t\) (fish/month), where \(t\) is months from the start. Find the net change in the number of fish over the 6 months. Click to reveal solution Net rate of change is \(B(t) - D(t) = 150 - 15 t\). \[ \int_0^6 (150 - 15 t)\, dt = \left[150 t - \tfrac{15}{2} t^2\right]_0^6 = 900 - \tfrac{15}{2}(36) = 900 - 270 = 630 \text{ fish}. \] Net gain = 630 fish over the six months. Arrivals beat deaths the whole time, but the gap was closing: the two rates would be equal at \(t = 10\) months. Problem 6: Total Biomass in a Riparian Strip A riparian strip is modeled as a rectangular region \(R = [0, 200] \times [0, 50]\) meters along a river bank. The biomass density is \[ \rho(x, y) = 5 + 0.01\,x \cdot y \quad \text{(kg/m}^2\text{)}, \] where \(x\) is distance along the bank and \(y\) is distance perpendicular from the bank. Find the total biomass in the strip. Click to reveal solution \[ \iint_R \rho(x, y)\, dA = \int_0^{200}\int_0^{50} (5 + 0.01\, x y)\, dy\, dx. \] Inner integral (over \(y\)): \[ \int_0^{50} (5 + 0.01\, x y)\, dy = \left[5 y + 0.005\, x y^2\right]_0^{50} = 250 + 0.005\, x (2500) = 250 + 12.5\, x. \] Outer integral (over \(x\)): \[ \int_0^{200} (250 + 12.5\, x)\, dx = \left[250\, x + 6.25\, x^2\right]_0^{200} = 50{,}000 + 6.25(40{,}000) = 50{,}000 + 250{,}000 = 300{,}000 \text{ kg}. \] Total biomass = 300,000 kg = 300 metric tons. Problem 7: Dissolved Oxygen Mass in a Lake Subsection A small lake subsection occupies the rectangular region \([0, 100] \times [0, 80]\) meters with a uniform depth of 5 meters. Dissolved oxygen concentration is modeled as \[ c(x, y) = 8 - 0.02\,x \quad \text{(mg/L)}, \] varying only with \(x\) (distance from the inflow). Assuming concentration doesn’t vary with depth, find the total mass of dissolved oxygen in the subsection. (Hint: 1 L = 0.001 m³.) Click to reveal solution Volume of the subsection: \(100 \times 80 \times 5 = 40{,}000\) m³ = \(4 \times 10^7\) L. Concentration averaged over \(x\): \[ \bar{c} = \frac{1}{100}\int_0^{100}(8 - 0.02\,x)\,dx = \frac{1}{100}\left[8\,x - 0.01\,x^2\right]_0^{100} = \frac{1}{100}(800 - 100) = 7 \text{ mg/L}. \] Total mass: \(7 \text{ mg/L} \times 4 \times 10^7 \text{ L} = 2.8 \times 10^8\) mg = 280 kg of dissolved oxygen. Problem 8: Numerical Integration of Hourly Evapotranspiration Data A weather station reports the following hourly evapotranspiration rates (mm/hr) for an 8-hour midday window: Hour 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 ET (mm/hr) 0.1 0.3 0.6 0.9 1.0 0.9 0.6 0.3 0.1 Use the trapezoidal rule with \(\Delta t = 1\) hr to estimate the total evapotranspiration over the 8-hour window. Click to reveal solution Trapezoidal rule: \[ \text{Total} \approx \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\bigl[f_0 + 2f_1 + 2f_2 + \cdots + 2f_7 + f_8\bigr]. \] \[ \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[0.1 + 2(0.3 + 0.6 + 0.9 + 1.0 + 0.9 + 0.6 + 0.3) + 0.1\bigr] = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[0.2 + 2(4.6)\bigr] = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.4) = 4.7 \text{ mm}. \] Total ET ≈ 4.7 mm over the 8-hour window. (Notice the symmetry: the data are roughly bell-shaped around the midday peak.) Problem 9: Average Pollutant Concentration in a Water Column A pollutant concentration in a 10-meter water column is modeled as \[ c(z) = 4 + 0.1\,z^2 \quad \text{(mg/L)}, \] where \(z\) is depth in meters from the surface. Find the average concentration over the 10-meter column. Click to reveal solution \[ \bar{c} = \frac{1}{10}\int_0^{10}(4 + 0.1\,z^2)\,dz = \frac{1}{10}\left[4 z + \tfrac{0.1}{3}\,z^3\right]_0^{10} = \frac{1}{10}\left(40 + \tfrac{100}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{10}\left(\tfrac{120 + 100}{3}\right) = \frac{220}{30} \approx 7.33 \text{ mg/L}. \] Average concentration ≈ 7.33 mg/L. The bottom water is much higher (\(c(10) = 14\) mg/L), but the cleaner upper water pulls the average down. Problem 10: Choose and Apply, Carbon Uptake Over a Growing Season A young Douglas-fir stand’s daily carbon uptake (photosynthesis) is modeled as \[ U(t) = 12 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi (t - 30)}{150}\right) \quad \text{(g C / m}^2\text{/day)}, \] where \(t\) is days from January 1. The model only applies between \(t = 30\) and \(t = 180\), roughly February through June, where \(U(t) \geq 0\). (That’s a simplification: Pacific Northwest conifers can fix some carbon for much of the year.) Find the total carbon uptake per square meter over that window. Before computing, decide whether this is an always-positive accumulation, a net accumulation or an average-value problem. Say why. Click to reveal solution Classification: always-positive accumulation. The window is restricted to where \(U(t) \geq 0\), and you want the total carbon fixed, not an average rate or a net. Compute the integral: \[ \int_{30}^{180} 12\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi(t-30)}{150}\right) dt. \] Let \(u = \frac{\pi(t-30)}{150}\), so \(du = \frac{\pi}{150}dt\), or \(dt = \frac{150}{\pi}du\). When \(t = 30\), \(u = 0\); when \(t = 180\), \(u = \pi\). \[ = 12 \cdot \tfrac{150}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi}\sin(u)\,du = \tfrac{1800}{\pi}\bigl[-\cos(u)\bigr]_0^{\pi} = \tfrac{1800}{\pi}\bigl(-(-1) - (-1)\bigr) = \tfrac{1800}{\pi}(2) = \tfrac{3600}{\pi} \approx 1146 \text{ g C / m}^2. \] Total carbon uptake ≈ 1146 g C/m² ≈ 1.15 kg C/m² over the growing season.
